articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos didn’t say earning P96 a day means Filipinos aren’t poor
articles.summary: While the P96-per-day threshold comes from actual statistical data, there are no reports that show Marcos saying it

blocks.text: Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said that people who make P96 a day are not considered poor.
Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user David Dodong posted a supposed quote card of Marcos bearing the claim.
The quote reads, “Kapag kumikita ka ng 96 pesos kada araw ay hindi ka na maituturing na mahirap.” (If you earn P96 a day, you can no longer be considered poor.)
While the post garnered only 204 reactions, 210 comments, and 33 shares, multiple commenters believed the claim.
Meanwhile, some criticized Marcos’ mental state. One Facebook user said that Marcos should experience life among the poor and see if P96 is enough.
Similar versions of the quote card have also been circulating online.
The facts: No official records or statements say that Marcos uttered these words. The fake quote was an altered version of another trending post that carried the claim while lacking context.

Source of the claim: Facebook user Panda Reports posted the same statement with Marcos’ photo, but attributed the quote to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) and the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev). The post had more than 430,000 reactions, 45,000 comments, and 67,000 shares as of writing.

In the comments section, the post author linked a video of Kamanggagawa Party-list Representative Eli San Fernando as the claim’s source. In the video, however, he asked for people’s reactions to the P96-per-day baseline.

Poverty threshold: The number came from the PSA’s 2025 poverty statistics, which showed the national poverty threshold at P35,121 per person a year, or about P2,927 a month. Per day, the threshold is approximately P96.
The PSA defines the poverty threshold as the minimum income or expenditure needed to meet the basic food and non-food requirements such as education, housing, health, clothing, and more.
A family or individual earning slightly more than that would no longer be considered poor, even if it means little room for savings, emergencies, or a good quality of life.

Current poverty statistics: In an August 24 statement, Finance Secretary Ralph Recto said that Marcos had ordered the government to “support the middle class and prevent 6.5 million Filipinos from sliding back into the zone of poverty.”

However, Marcos, the PSA, and DEPDev did not mention or suggest that P96 a day is enough to maintain a comfortable and decent lifestyle. As 28% of Filipinos live just above the poverty line, a big blow to one’s lifestyle — like job loss, price spikes, or natural disasters — might just be what it takes to push them back under it.

The same poverty statistics showed that the number of Filipinos living below the poverty threshold fell from 17.5 million in 2023 to 11.08 million in 2025. As a result, nearly 6.5 million Filipinos have been lifted out of poverty. – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: NAPOLCOM probes Rizal cop over alleged abuse of ex-partner, other misconduct
articles.summary: The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) on Friday said it will investigate a police officer in Rizal accused of abusing his former live-in partner, as well as other alleged misconduct during his…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 3:42pm

The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) on Friday said it will investigate a police officer in Rizal accused of abusing his former live-in partner, as well as other alleged misconduct during his service.

At a press briefing, NAPOLCOM Commissioner Rafael Vicente Calinisan said the Commission's Inspection, Monitoring, and Investigation Service (IMIS) would immediately look into the allegations against the police officer.

The complainant, a woman from Antipolo City, Rizal, accused the cop of physical assault, threats involving a firearm, verbal harassment, intimidation, and financial control during their relationship, which began in 2016 and ended in 2020.

She also alleged that the police officer pressured her to terminate her pregnancy, while the prolonged abuse reportedly took a toll on her mental health, resulting in a diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
The woman said she had previously filed seven criminal, civil, and administrative complaints against the cop but he remained in active police service.

"Talagang susuriin natin ito at iimbestigahan nang maayos. Napakahaba ng litanya ng pang-aabuso. Hindi lamang ito nakaaapekto sa kanyang pamilya kundi pati sa serbisyo niya sa ordinaryong tao," Calinisan said.
"We will make sure that policemen like this will be brought to justice," he added.
The complaint also raised allegations of misconduct when the police officer was assigned as a jailer in Antipolo.

According to the complainant, the cop allegedly had a supposed "boss" among persons deprived of liberty (PDLs), whom he reportedly allowed to leave detention and who allegedly gave him money and a pickup vehicle.
He was also accused of negligence in connection with the escape of a detainee.
NAPOLCOM said IMIS would validate these allegations and investigate the cop's previous assignment in jail, particularly the alleged negligence involving the detainee's escape.
The police officer had previously faced administrative proceedings before the PNP Internal Affairs Service (IAS), which initially dismissed him from the service.
However, upon reconsideration, the penalty was reportedly reduced to a 60-day suspension after he cited his desire to see their child.
He was reassigned from the Taytay Municipal Police Station to the Binangonan Municipal Police Station in September 2024.
The complainant also alleged that the police officer cheated during examinations under his PNP Field Training Program by photographing examination questions and sending them to her for answers.
She claimed she would answer the questions and send the answers back to the police officer while he was taking the examinations.
Calinisan immediately directed IMIS to investigate the allegations, including how examinations are conducted in the PNP Training Service.
"Napakaseryosong alegasyon niyan. Pinipicturan ang examination, ipinapadala ang mga tanong sa ibang tao sa labas, at binibigyan ng sagot ang examinee habang nagsasagawa ng pagsusulit," he said.
GMA News Online has reached out to Binangonan Municipal Police Station for the side of the police officer, but it has yet to respond as of posting time. —AOL, GMA News

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from across India on Friday, November 6.
November 6, 2026
Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam turn to top court for bail, citing stalled witness testimony
Activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam approached the Supreme Court on Thursday for bail once again in the 2020 Delhi riots "larger conspiracy" case.
They are challenging a September 30 Delhi High Court order that rejected their pleas, Bar and Bench reported. The pleas had not yet been listed for hearing.

The High Court held that judicial discipline bound it to the Supreme Court's January 5 order and that it could not alter the terms set there. In that order, the top court refused bail to the two while granting relief to five co-accused, saying they "stand on a qualitatively different footing as compared to other accused," local media reported.
The ruling allowed them to reapply once the protected witnesses had been examined or a year had passed, whichever came first.

Imam says he has spent six years and nine months in jail as an undertrial without the prosecution examining any of its 47 protected witnesses, Live Law reported. He argues the witness condition is therefore unlikely to be met in time.

blocks.caption: Sharjeel Imam was arrested in January 2020 and has remained in undertrial detention for nearly seven yearsImage: Dinesh Joshi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The pleas also say over 900 witnesses are yet to be examined and that continued imprisonment violates the right to life and liberty under Article 21.
On May 18, another Supreme Court bench criticized the January order, observing that "bail is the rule and jail is an exception" even under the anti-terror law UAPA.
Delhi Police have described the two as "masterminds" of the violence that took place in February 2020. However, nearly seven years later, the trial has not yet begun.

In a statement on Friday, November 6, NPC spokesperson and Deputy Privacy Commissioner Jose Belarmino II said “the Commission has not received personal data breach notifications from the concerned government agencies in relation to the reported incidents.”

The NPC said it will coordinate directly with any identified government agencies to “verify the alleged incidents, ascertain the circumstances surrounding them, and determine whether personal data have been compromised.”

“Where warranted, the Commission will require the concerned agencies to submit the necessary reports and comply with their obligations under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and applicable NPC issuances,” the NPC added.

Vice President’s scheduling system
Department of Labor and Employment Public Employment Service Office

Bataan’s internal government website

blocks.text: Also reportedly affected were a number of other systems, such as Eastern Visayas State University, as well as nongovernment entities such as the Philippine Nurses Association, Alliance Graduate School, and Luzviminda Construction and Development Corporation.

blocks.text: The NPC added in its statement that “reports of alleged data leaks do not, by themselves, establish that a personal data breach has occurred or that the provisions of the Data Privacy Act of 2012 have been violated.”

articles.title: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
articles.summary: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
articles.byline: Shayan Sardarizadeh, Benedict Garman, Matt Murphy

blocks.text: Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst noted that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

articles.title: Filipino teens among least physically active in the world -- study
articles.summary: Filipino adolescents are among the least physically active in the world, ranking seventh among all countries and topping the ranks in Southeast Asia, according to a study published Wednesday in The…

blocks.text: Filipino adolescents are among the least physically active in the world, ranking seventh among all countries and topping the ranks in Southeast Asia, according to a study published Wednesday in The Lancet medical journal.

The study examined surveys on the active days of adolescents aged 11 to 17 years across 195 countries from 2010 to 2025. An active day is defined as reporting at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity a day.
Among all countries, the Philippines ranked seventh with 40.32% of Filipino adolescents having zero active days. More Filipino girls (42.7%) reported this compared to Filipino boys (38.0%).
Nepal topped the global list, followed by Zimbabwe, Nauru, Mauritania, Tuvalu, Namibia, and the Philippines.
Countries with the lowest mean active days were five nations in South and Southeast Asia.

"Those with the lowest mean active days were five countries in South and Southeast Asia (Cambodia, Philippines, Timor-Leste, Viet Nam, and Nepal), four in sub-Saharan Africa (Gabon, Liberia, Madagascar, and Mauritania), and Jordan," it said.

This contrasts with countries reporting the highest mean active days, located in Central and Eastern Europe, Central Asia, and high-income Western regions, including Serbia, Canada, Ireland, Kazakhstan, and Finland.

Overall, the study revealed that one in five adolescents globally, or 24.9%, reported zero active days per week. Meanwhile, only one in seven adolescents, or 13.9%, recorded active days all seven days of the week.

In 2018, World Health Organization (WHO) member-states adopted a global target of a 15% relative reduction in physical inactivity by 2030—a goal the report says cannot be met if current trends continue.
"If the 2010–25 trends continue until 2030, the global target will not be met," the report said.
Girls left behind
By sex, female teens reported fewer active days and a higher prevalence of zero active days than males globally.
Globally, 21.7% of boys reported zero active days, compared to 28.4% of girls.
Consequently, a higher proportion of boys recorded active days in all seven days of the week compared to girls, at 16.7% and 11%, respectively.
"Physical activity also declined across adolescence among girls, further widening disparities," the study noted.
Physical activity vs. nation's wealth
A country's income level was among the key factors discussed in the study, which identified patterns in the active days of adolescents based on economic setting.
High-income countries generally showed a higher proportion of adolescents who had active days three or more times a week.

"We identified two distinct patterns of active days that are broadly aligned with country income. In most low-income and middle-income settings, patterns were characterised by high prevalence of 0 active days and low mean active days," the study said.

"By contrast, high-income western, central and eastern Europe and central Asia, and east Asia and the Pacific regions showed a more favourable distribution, with fewer adolescents reporting 0–2 active days and more reporting 3 or more active days," it added.

This finding is likely influenced by disparities in access to opportunities and supportive environments, such as those provided "through school, community programmes, infrastructure (eg, public open spaces), and safe walking and cycling networks."
"Wealthier countries might dedicate resources to ensure quality implementation of relevant policies, increasing opportunities for adolescents to be active," the study said.
Implications

The high level of physical inactivity among adolescents carries critical implications for national policies and practices. The report underscored that a high prevalence of zero active days indicates that existing interventions are failing to reach a significant portion of the adolescent population.

The report also emphasized the importance of tailoring policies to local environments and sociocultural contexts. For instance, areas with high levels of non-participation are recommended to focus on creating environments that support physical activity across everyday settings.
With regard to gender and age disparities, the study explained that the sharp decline in active days among girls highlights the need for more gender-responsive policies and programs.

"Programmes and policies focused solely on individual behaviour change are unlikely to be sufficient without parallel action to address barriers to girls' activity, including restrictive gender norms, safety concerns, and lack of opportunities that meet girls' needs and preferences," the study added.
It also highlighted the critical role of schools, which serve as the primary setting for adolescents and the place where they should be given more opportunities to stay active.

"Schools are often a central setting for intervention, but evidence of effectiveness is mixed, possibly due to implementation challenges in complex school systems. Where impact has been demonstrated, programmes have typically been multicomponent," the report said.
"Engaging young people in co-creation of strategies might strengthen ownership, acceptability, and Sustainability," it added.
Creating the environment
For its part, the WHO stressed the importance of creating environments where physical activity becomes a normal and effortless part of daily life.
The organization emphasized the need for more effective national policies and stronger policy implementation in schools.
The WHO called for urgent, coordinated action across the education, transport, urban planning, sport, and health sectors, alongside targeted efforts to address the multiple barriers faced by girls.
"The challenge is not simply to persuade adolescents to move more. It is to create environments that make being active a normal and easy part of growing up," WHO said.

"Countries need policies that make physical activity an easy, safe and accessible part of everyday life. Promoting physical activity in schools, investing in safe walking and cycling routes, and creating more active communities can give young people more opportunities to move, play and be active in their everyday lives," it added. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Senate impeachment court admits prosecution evidence in Sara Duterte trial
articles.summary: The defense earlier challenged the admissibility of the prosecution's documentary evidence

items: The Senate impeachment court has allowed the admission of most documentary evidence presented by the prosecution against Vice President Sara Duterte, overruling defense objections regarding the evidence's acquisition and relevance.
The court emphasized that pre-incumbency records could only be used to establish a factual baseline for evaluating Duterte's financial status during her term
The court reinstated the sub judice ruling, prohibiting public comments on the impeachment trial, and the proceedings will resume on November 9 with the defense team presenting their evidence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court has overruled the defense’s objections to the documentary evidence presented by the prosecution in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, allowing the admission of most of the contested records, subject to certain limitations.

“The Court overrules the continuing objection founded on the non-attachment of the offered exhibits to the Impeachment Complaints or Articles of Impeachment and on their acquisition through subpoenas during trial,” the decision dated Thursday, November 5, read.

In its comment on the House prosecution panel’s formal offer of evidence, the defense challenged the admissibility of the subpoenaed documents, reiterating its claim that the records were obtained through an “impermissible fishing expedition.”

The impeachment court, however, said characterizing the process as such did not, by itself, constitute grounds for excluding the evidence. It added that the exhibits remained subject to tests of relevance and competence, as well as applicable confidentiality and authentication requirements.

Article 2, which concerns allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte, is the only remaining impeachment article against the Vice President after the House prosecution panel withdrew the three other articles.

In its ruling, the court allowed the admission of Duterte’s records from 2007 to 2021, but limited their use to establishing a factual baseline “against which the Respondent’s assets, liabilities, net worth, financial resources, transactions, and business interests during 2022 to 2025 may be evaluated under Article II.”

The court stressed that the pre-incumbency records could not be used to charge or establish any separate impeachable offense committed before Duterte assumed office as vice president. Neither could they establish liability for conduct outside the scope of Article II or revive any of the withdrawn articles.

“Verily, no pre-incumbency record can be admitted to merely suggest any habit or propensity to violate the law when such habit or propensity is in the first place irrelevant to the Article in issue,” the ruling said.

Among the admitted evidence were Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), bank and insurance records, and documents from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS), and Land Registration Authority (LRA).

Also admitted were records from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), which the court said could establish that the identified reports — including intelligence reports, covered transaction reports (CTRs), and suspicious transaction reports (STRs) — were filed or issued to Duterte. It could also establish the transaction flows reflected in them, insofar as these were relevant to Article 2.

The court also admitted Duterte’s bank and tax records to establish reported income, assets, and business interests. Insurance and investment records were admitted to establish relevant policy, investment, ownership, payment, and account particulars, “which may be compared with the SALNs and other financial records under Article II.”
“Their attribution, valuation, required disclosure, and evidentiary weight remain for final evaluation,” the ruling added.

Meanwhile, the impeachment court excluded corporate records of the JTC Group of Companies Philippines Incorporated and Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corporation, including entries, summaries, schedules, and computations derived from those records in other exhibits.

It also excluded a portion of the forensic financial report of lawyer Alex Cabrera concerning the two corporate entities but admitted the remainder of his analysis. The court, however, clarified the validity of the report’s assumptions, methodology, totals, and inferences remains subject to the senator-judges’ final evaluation.

The impeachment court also excluded the Commission on Audit (COA) findings and notices of disallowance involving confidential fund disbursements by the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education in 2022 and 2023 as it was offered in connection with Article 1, one of the withdrawn impeachment articles.

“Admission does not, ipso facto, establish the truth or accuracy of any such evidence, nor does it constitute an adoption by this Court of any conclusion of law framed by the Prosecution in its Formal Offer,” the ruling said.
“The evidentiary weight and sufficiency of every admitted exhibit remain exclusively for the Senator-Judges to determine upon final deliberation,” it added.
With the resolution of the prosecution’s formal offer of documentary evidence, the impeachment court said the prosecution had formally rested its case-in-chief on Article II.

In a separate decision, the impeachment court ruled to reinstate the imposition of Rule 18 on the Rules of Procedure on Impeachment Trial on all Articles of Impeachment against Duterte, including those withdrawn or pending adjudication.

This developed after the defense counsel objected to abandoning the sub judice ruling on the withdrawn articles, saying that doing this midway into the trial could undermine the integrity of the proceedings.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero ordered the strict enforcement of the rule in August, prohibiting all involved parties including the presiding officer, senator-judges, prosecutors, the respondent, their counsel, as well as all witnesses from making comments or disclosing the merits of the case of the ongoing impeachment trial in public or online.

“The sub judice principle under Rule 18 of the Rules of Procedure on Impeachment Trials shall apply with equal force to all articles of impeachment whether withdrawn or pending adjudication,” the November 5 ruling said.

“To uphold and reiterate the August 26, 2026 ruling of the Presiding Officer on the application of Rule 18 and enjoin all persons covered thereunder to refrain from making, issuing, or otherwise promoting any public statement or commentary concerning the merits of the pending trial or any matter encompassed by the Articles of Impeachment filed with this Court,” it added.

The impeachment proceedings were put on hold to give way to Senate committee hearings on the proposed 2027 national budget. It will resume on Monday, November 9, with Duterte’s defense team beginning its presentation of evidence. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: The size of the stockpile of H200 chips, which has not previously been reported, reflects Beijing's reluctance to increase reliance on US technology

items: Approximately 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are stored in Hong Kong, pending approval from Beijing for large-scale imports to mainland China, despite high demand from Chinese tech firms.

China has allowed limited entry of H200 chips, with some companies obtaining small quantities, but large-volume imports remain unapproved, reflecting Beijing's concerns over reliance on US technology.
The H200 chip, while not the most advanced, is crucial for AI training in China, leading to increased prices in the unofficial market due to US export controls and Beijing's restrictions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

About 600,000 of Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips are stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to mainland China, two people familiar with the matter said, as Beijing withholds approval for large-scale imports despite demand from tech firms.
The size of the stockpile of H200 chips, which has not previously been reported, reflects Beijing’s reluctance to increase reliance on US technology.
At the same time, Chinese companies need Nvidia’s advanced computing power to meet surging AI demand in the world’s second-largest economy.

China has allowed entry for some of the chips in recent months, three people familiar with the matter said. Several major Chinese internet companies have each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips in the past few months, one of the people said.
Three people said small quantities of chips had been shipped via intermediaries and indirect routes without specifying how many. The Hong Kong government did not respond to a request for comment.
But Beijing has yet to approve large-volume imports into mainland China, the people said.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the National Development and Reform Commission did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Nvidia or Chinese tech companies Alibaba, ByteDance, DeepSeek and Tencent.

The H200 is not Nvidia’s newest AI processor, but it has capabilities that Chinese alternatives have yet to match, making it useful for training AI models particularly when combined with Nvidia’s software.
US export controls since 2022 have sought to restrict China’s access to advanced Nvidia chips and the equipment needed to make them.
With authorized supply constrained, Chinese buyers have turned to intermediaries and indirect routes, pushing up prices in the unofficial market.

An eight-card H200 server was offered for more than 6 million yuan ($900,000) in mainland China by the end of October, about three times its price a year earlier, one person familiar with the matter said. Servers using Nvidia’s newer Blackwell chips, which fall under US export controls, were offered for more than 20 million yuan apiece, the person added.
The H200 chip is caught in tension over trade and technology more broadly between Washington and Beijing.

The United States barred exports of the H200 to China before President Donald Trump’s administration gave Nvidia permission last year to sell the chips to approved Chinese customers. The policy shift followed US-China trade negotiations.
Reuters reported in May that the US had approved H200 chip sales to 10 Chinese firms, including Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance.
But Beijing has imposed its own constraints on H200 imports, reflecting concerns about dependence on US technology.

Technology publication, the Information, reported in July that Chinese officials had told companies, including Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek that they could receive permission to buy limited quantities of H200 chips for training AI models.
It reported that total approvals could amount to fewer than 200,000 chips and that Beijing wanted firms to prioritise Chinese processors for inference — the task of running AI models.

Reuters reported last month that ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent had ordered more than 3 million Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards, a less powerful export-compliant product, with a combined sticker price exceeding $35 billion. – Rappler.com

articles.title: M&S takes on John Lewis in Christmas ad battle with topless ‘shredded Santa’
articles.summary:
James Norton and Lucy Punch star as a youthful Mr and Mrs Claus in lively ad about shared moments as well as shopping

For years the “Christmas advert moment” has belonged to one brand. John…

blocks.text: For years the “Christmas advert moment” has belonged to one brand. John Lewis’s syrupy commercials featuring piano ballads and tearjerker storylines have given the 160-year-old department store a cultural head start in the dash for festive profits.

This year, however, there’s one high-street rival with a sackful of tricks to make up the ground. Marks & Spencer has brought out the big guns – in the form of a topless Santa, played by the small-screen heart-throb James Norton.

The lively M&S Christmas ad has already drawn comparisons with John Lewis’s effort, which features Kristin Scott Thomas as a glamorous granny on the hunt to turn one room of her huge townhouse into a fun “gran cave”.
In the M&S corner Norton and Lucy Punch play a youthful Mr and Mrs Claus – with a lingering shot of Norton with his top off.
When John Lewis launched its advert this week, its portrayal of wealth was criticised, with a sprawling house and ungrateful grandchildren said to be out of touch with the wider mood of the nation.

But shots of Norton topless aside from an M&S white cotton towel have gone viral. Men’s Health magazine described him as a “shredded Santa”, saying his Saint Nick “leaves the traditional mince-pie physique looking a little dated”.

blocks.caption: The ‘shredded Santa’: James Norton wears just a white M&S cotton towel.  Photograph: M&S

blocks.text: Gurjit Degun, the creativity and cultural editor at Campaign, a business magazine that covers advertising and marketing, described the M&S ad as “playful and tongue in cheek without being silly”.

M&S has combined its fashion, food, beauty and homeware strands into one campaign rather than individual adverts, a strategy it last used in 2017. Norton plays an undercover Santa who shaves off his beard so he can experience the buildup to Christmas incognito, while Punch is a snobbish Mrs Claus, similar to her character in Amandaland.

After the couple gatecrash a dinner party, swing by a children’s carol service and discover “picky bits”, the key takeaway from M&S is that Christmas is about shared moments rather than just big gifts. Although of course the advert is very much about shopping. Every element of it – from Punch’s pyjamas to that towel and the prawn cones Norton said he saw “hundreds” of during filming – is available to buy. Meanwhile, the main message derived from the John Lewis campaign is to give physical gifts rather than cold, hard cash.

Norton said the combination of a “playful, funny and reverent script” appealed to him. He is a “huge fan” of the advert’s director, Shannon Murphy, who has worked on shows including Killing Eve and Babyteeth.

blocks.caption: ‘I want fun and joy,’ said Lucy Punch. Photograph: M&S

blocks.text: “I trusted that Shannon would deliver on the tone,” he said. “She’s such a cool cat.” While he is usually “a sucker for a traditional tearjerker”, he believes the ad still captures the emotion of Christmas thanks to those family-and-friends moments that speak to “connection and joy”.

Punch said she liked the deliberately humorous script. “I don’t want any more Christmas tearjerkers,” she said. “I want fun and joy. Life is enough of a tearjerker, it’s fun to have something festive with a bit of a wink.”

In a tough consumer market, there is a lot weighing on the adverts’ success for the retailers. M&S is still trying to bounce back from a 2025 cyber hack that forced it to close its website for more than six weeks, costing it over £100m; John Lewis is trying to revive interest as it grapples with higher costs alongside a decline in consumer confidence.

blocks.caption: Kristin Scott Thomas in the John Lewis Christmas ad: she represents a target customer.  Photograph: John Lewis/PA

blocks.text: Jonathan De Mello, the founder of JDM Retail consulting, describes the John Lewis strategy as smart, explaining that the casting of Scott Thomas reflected the type of customer the retailer was trying to appeal to.

“They are targeting a group that is fairly affluent,” he said. “They have a decent chunk of disposable income because they have paid off their mortgages.” However, this approach could “alienate the mass market”, he cautioned, as for a younger generation “it portrays a type of lifestyle that for many is unattainable”.

The M&S advert is a reflection of how the retailer has successfully turned its business around, De Mello said. “Before, there was a dichotomy between the food and the fashion, and now they are very much aligned. M&S now taps into the younger consumer psyche and this advert reflects this.”

articles.title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
articles.summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".

blocks.text: Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".

Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.

Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.

He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".

Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.

Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.

Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

articles.title: A movie tour, a “safetynovela,” and other winners at Boomerang Awards 2026
articles.summary: It’s a celebration of creativity — and wit

blocks.text: It’s a celebration of creativity — and wit

items: The Boomerang Awards 2026, organized by the Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines, showcased innovative digital marketing campaigns from Southeast Asia, emphasizing creativity as a valuable currency.

Notable winners included BBDO Guerrero's 'Safetynovela' campaign for Philippine Airlines and the 'Some Nights I Feel Like Doing a Grindr Movie Tour' by the Lennon Group, in partnership with Lunchbox Studios, both recognized for their unique approaches to engaging audiences.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines (DMAP) and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.
Creativity as a currency has never been this valuable.

Our trust issues with creative work continue to grow every day as we question a poster’s level of slop or a viral video’s clear seal of originality. But on the flip side, there’s been a silver lining: this phenomenon has been a go-signal for brands to prove their uniqueness, and moreover, their own hard work that makes things happen.
After all, the recently concluded DigiCon 2026 highlighted the importance of AI as a collaborator, and not as a total replacement for human talent.

The two-day flagship event of the Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines drew in global leaders from the marketing, technology, and business industries, and concluded with the Boomerang Awards 2026, showcasing the best of digital marketing, advertising, and technology.

blocks.caption: Members of Rappler and The Nerve at the Boomerang Awards night

blocks.text: This year’s Boomerang is extra significant as it expands beyond the Philippines with the celebration of campaigns done by Southeast Asian organizations. Leading the packed panel were jury presidents Geia Lopez, head of creative and creator partnerships at Google Southeast Asia; Theresa Ong, head of creative shop at Meta; VJ Anand, co-founder and chief creative officer at Ballsy; Erik Reiff, founding partner and chief creative officer at Black Cat White Cat; and Rey Tiempo, founder and chief creative officer and creative gaming specialist at Co-op Play.
The awardees were divided into five categories: Innovation in Digital Experience, Media, Entertainment, Craft, and Specializations.

One of the apparent threads of the gold winners nods to our local flavor. In fact, you’ve probably seen one of the winning entries on your recent flight: BBDO Guerrero’s “Safetynovela” campaign for Philippine Airlines.

blocks.caption: A movie tour, a “safetynovela,” and other winners at Boomerang Awards 2026

blocks.text: Rather than doing a run-of-the-mill instruction on in-flight safety, this campaign infuses the familiar Pinoy teleserye blueprint through characters, cinematography, music, and even tropes to effectively get passengers’ attention, while not losing sight of being informative. This creatively dramatic video bagged gold under both Digital Experience and Entertainment, and also nabbed a Grand Prix spot.

“Some Nights I Feel Like Doing a Grindr Movie Tour” by the Lennon Group, in partnership with Lunchbox Studios, also took home gold under the Innovation in Digital Experience, Media, and Craft categories. Originally a promotional material for queer Filipino indie film “Some Nights I Feel Like Walking” by Petersen Vargas, this fully immersive activation included actors touring in the social networking app and an unorthodox mall premiere.

Also among the Digital Experience gold winners is Kween Yasmin’s team-up with GIGIL for Canva Pro. Highlighting her position as the “all-purpose kween,” the campaign featured her own Creator Page where a specially designed font called Kween Sans and emoji set called Kweemoji can be enjoyed by the software’s users.

blocks.caption: The people behind the “Kween Yasmin” campaign by GIGIL x Canva Pro, winning gold for Innovation in Digital Experience

blocks.text: Some campaigns also play as answers to today’s concerns in online consumption, like the “Brain Unrot Library” created by Grey Malaysia in partnership with BookXcess. This anti-doomscrolling initiative reintroduces literary works and promotes reading focus through social-first storytelling.

Another gold winner of the night includes Octopus&Whale’s “GAMEJOY: The First Universal Gamer Money” campaign, which . This serves Jollibee Philippines’ customers with “eat-to-earn” in-game rewards, particularly those who play Mobile Legends: Bang Bang.
Other gold winners include “Gamifries” by Leo Manila x BBH Singapore for McDonald’s Philippines and “Play No Drew” by BBDO Guerrero for PepsiCo Philippines.

blocks.caption: Among the gold winners for Innovation in Digital Experience include “Gamifries” by Leo Manila and BBH Singapore for McDonald’s Philippines

blocks.text: For the full list of winners, including the silver and bronze awardees, head to the official Boomerang Awards website. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Friday briefing: ​After a week of disruption, is living with threats our new normal?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: From diverted airliners to hacked ​fridges, a string of disruptive incidents has exposed the ​vulnerabilities of modern ​life. ​There is now an increasingly blurred space…

blocks.text: Good morning. A multiplicity of hoax bomb threats divert passenger flights across Europe. A malign cyber-attack targets supermarket fridges in Belgium, Sweden, the UK and – in a sickening escalation – the cold storage facilities of France’s national blood service.

The actors behind this week of chaos and disruption, be they hostile states or criminal gangs – or even enterprising teenagers – are yet to be identified. But what is certain is that they operate in a context of deepening global conflicts, building national threat and an accompanying, pervasive sense of vulnerability.
Welcome to the grey zone – that ambiguous space between routine peace and conventional military conflict, where proxies duck state accountability and cyber-tactics are developing at an alarming rate.

For today’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s defence and security editor, Dan Sabbagh, and our global technology team about flights, fridges and why “keep calm and carry on” is more than a tote bag slogan.
But first the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK news | Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others over the course of five years of his show business career.

US politics | Donald Trump signed a proclamation that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.
UK politics | Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington.
Health | Cancer diagnoses in England have hit record highs, with more than 1,000 people a day diagnosed, NHS figures show.
World news | The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘Terrorism doesn’t have to be violent. The purpose is to scare’

blocks.caption: Attacking refrigeration systems that store blood products is a sinister but not immediate threat. Photograph: Lionel RAULT/EFS/AP

blocks.text: Hoax bomb threats disrupted at least 25 different commercial flights across Europe yesterday, with some forced to make emergency landings, and after similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes were searched or diverted after malicious alerts.

There is, at least so for, no suggestion of orchestration by a hostile terror group or state actor according to investigators, although investigations continue. It’s perfectly possible that this could be the work of some lone disruptors, says Dan, who reminds me that “airlines receive bomb threats on a daily basis, at a rate that we would find extraordinary if we knew”. Nonetheless, the fact that these airlines are treating these threats as credible suggests a potential level of coordination, aviation experts told the Guardian on Thursday.

These threats take place with aviation security under sharper scrutiny after the flydubai incident, when a pilot fought off his knife-wielding colleague in an apparent attempt to crash a full passenger flight heading for Tel Aviv.

But beyond that “jittery background noise”, is a significant step-change in the manner of threat we face. Twenty-five years on from the inception of the War on Terror, when Islamist terrorism has receded relative to the hostile state threats, “we’re living in a different world with familiar uncertainties, but attributed to different players,” Dan tells me.

Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East are reverberating closer to home. Since 2022, we’ve witnessed intensifying acts of sabotage on European states that are believed to trace back to Russia but deliberately fall below the threshold for military response – a so-called hybrid or “shadow war” with the singular purpose of disrupting support for Ukraine. Only two months ago, an alleged attack plot on RAF Fairford was organised by a handler police believe was working on behalf of Iran.

Meanwhile, tech expert Azeem Azhar warned recently that the internet is experiencing it’s own Wuhan moment, as AI enables bad actors to hunt for system flaws and spread them, mirroring the early days of the Covid pandemic.
“Terrorism doesn’t have to be violent to terrorise,” says Dan. “The purpose of terrorism is to scare.”
What about other targets?

Ratcheting up disruption, and the accompanying psychological hit, is precisely what we’ve seen elsewhere this week. Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this week, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C, in what some fear indicates a new front in hacking tactics.

Similar incidents have been reported in the UK, and I spoke to our global technology editor Dan Milmo on his way back from interviewing a fruit and veg wholesaler based near Heathrow, whose fridges went on the blink on Monday. The experience has prompted him to add some tinned goods to his weekend shopping list.

“There are only ever two likely candidates for a hack,” Dan tells me. “Criminal gangs or nation states.” He adds an emerging tertiary category of “troublesome teenagers”, such as the loose collective of English-speaking hackers Scattered Spider, two of whom were jailed in July for their attack on Transport for London.

One cybersecurity researcher told Dan that attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – one of the software systems also targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – had “all the hallmarks” of operations linked to Russia.
What are security services doing about these threats?

“There is a very real and intense cyberwar going on out there,” Dan Sabbagh tells me, and security agencies in the UK have viewed technological resilience as a key part of their responsibility for a number of years. The Turing Institute, for example, is looking at ways to utilise AI to make critical infrastructure systems more secure.

The police and security services are monitoring for threats all the time – MI5 has about 3,000 active subjects of interest currently – arranged in a hierarchy, with an understandable focus on the more serious ones, including threats to life. But lower level activity that is not obviously threatening, whether that’s online activity or buying paint with the intention of daubing racist graffiti, can be harder to pick up. As with other public services, this is a resourcing question as much as anything else.
Is chaos easier to generate in our interconnected world?

I put this to our global technology reporter Aisha Down, who explains that many hacks happen though edge devices – networked items that are connected to the internet but don’t have processing power and so aren’t the main focus of security upgrades by a company or household.
Famously, in 2016, North Korea came within a few keystrokes of pulling off a billion-dollar heist by hacking the Bank of Bangladesh via an unsecured printer.

Aisha is keen to dial down the panic. The point about cyber-attacks is that every single one is opportunistic: a hacker has to find a vulnerability and then discover a way to exploit it. “Just like a burglary, you might get into the room where all the jewellery is stored,” she says, “but the damage you can do is not a given.”

There is, however, a steady escalation in this type of threat. Aisha gives the example of Finland which, given its proximity to Russia, is watching cyber-tactics very closely. “What people report to their national cybersecurity centre is growing, from 18,000 reports last year for a population of 6 million people, to 21,000 this year.” This can be partly traced back to a developing criminal hacking ecosystem, some with loose links to the Russian state.
Do we need to buy more beans?

While a key element of a cyber-attack is the psychological impact, that can be hard to square with the UK government’s own Be Ready initiative, which advises us to off-set threats of hybrid warfare and hostile state sabotage by stockpiling 72 hours’ worth of emergency supplies – including water, beans and Twiglets (if you’re Andy Burnham). Indeed, governments across Europe are advising citizens to build up non-perishable larders.
It’s perhaps useful to balance the likelihood of a cyber-attack with the potential scope, suggests Aisha, who confesses she’s too busy sourcing furniture for her new flat to think about tinned goods.
One European cybersecurity official told Aisha recently that there’s a vulnerability in every 1,500 lines of code, on average.
“Their view is: it’s going to happen. It’s going to be opportunistic. But, unlike bombing a power station in the dead of winter, you won’t be offline for months.”
With that perspective, keeping a bunch of tenners handy to see you through a few days of disruption makes sense.

As for stockpiling food and water, Dan is still debating with his partner just how necessary those extra tins of peas really are. “If you’re a government wanting to spend £10bn more on defence by the end of the decade, it’s useful to have that message about keeping a few bottles of water at home,” he says.

To be clear: it’s not Dan’s intention to dismiss stockpiling advice as a purely cynical exercise. The developing threats are all too real. But as he puts it: “If the purpose of terrorism is to generate fear, the first thing you should do is not panic and keep calm.”

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: Will the UK finally pay slavery reparations?

Andy Burnham has asked countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape a formal apology through a ‘structured dialogue’. During the prime minister’s visit to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, Downing Street said affected countries would play an indispensable role in crafting an enduring message. Though the plans for talks were received positively, the British government is still ruling out the idea of paying reparations, which for decades campaigners have been calling for. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan.

blocks.text: On 25 October, as Brazil held its presidential election, 101-year-old Celia de Oliveira Soares left home for the first time in months, to vote for the first time in nearly a decade. She was determined that Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known as Lula) – who had lost in the first round – should beat the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

Since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s, no first-round loser has ever bounced back. But 3 million extra voters took part in the second round, after skipping the first – and 1.4 million of them were over 70 years old. The victorious Lula, along with many others, is now hailing elderly voters as the election’s heroes.
“It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” the former minister Simone Tebet said. “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”

articles.title: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch
articles.summary:
Federal judge issues 14-day restraining order on any construction work on Washington monument, hours after it was approved by planning commission

A federal judge has halted construction work…

blocks.text: A federal judge has halted construction work on Donald Trump’s towering triumphal arch for 14 days, a major setback for one of the president’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.

The temporary restraining order was issued by US district judge Tanya Chutkan in the early hours of Friday. It followed a series of steps taken on Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the 250-foot-high (76-meter) arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a nine-hour hearing where dozens of witnesses opposed the construction.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats gained control of Congress.

The administration had said the work on the arch could begin as soon as the approval and the interior department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.

In issuing the delay, Chutkan granted the request of the latest plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch. Chutkan also consolidated lawsuits from the District of Columbia and Virginia with a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian.
It’s unclear how much the project will cost, or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100m.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump holds up a model for his proposed arch back in October 2025.   Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The vote by the planning commission on Thursday came after nine and a half hours and scores of people opposing it. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor work for the administration or are connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.

The remote, call-in hearing – which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section – drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch that they said would destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington national cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.
The panel’s Trump-appointed chair launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chair.

As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.

Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”

But DC city council member Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project had not received required approval from Congress, nor had Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.

“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans, as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.

articles.title: Kapunan: VP Sara is best evidence against herself
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is the best evidence against herself, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said Friday.

blocks.text: IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published November 6, 2026 2:31pm
Vice President Sara Duterte is the best evidence against herself, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said Friday.

Kapunan made the response when asked if the Vice President taking the witness stand will enable the Vice President to answer the impeachable allegations leveled against her, mainly amassing around P817 million worth of unexplained wealth.

“If the Vice President appears before the impeachment court, she will be the best evidence against herself due to her demeanor, the way she answers. Remember, when she was summoned in House [hearings], she refused to take an oath. Would she even take an oath to tell the truth and nothing but the truth?” Kapunan said.

“The only one she can blame is herself. She gave evidence against herself by declaring her in her SALN interest in these companies,” Kapunan said, referring to declared assets of the Vice President such as Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and GenCorp. Foods Industries Inc. which Duterte has not divested from even amid a Constitutional prohibition.
GMA News Online has reached out to Duterte's spokesperson Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. for comment but he has yet to reply as of posting time.

Back in September, the House prosecution panel intended to present Duterte in her own impeachment trial. But Kapunan later on said that given that the previous hostile witness from the Office of the Vice President merely said they "do not know" or were unaware of the allegations, it is likely that the Vice President will do the same.

Ahead of Kapunan’s pronouncements, the Senate impeachment court earlier admitted Vice President Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) in all the years she was public official since 2007, as well as the bank account, bank transaction and corporate records under her name and her husband Manases Carpio, into the list of evidence for her impeachment trial.
The impeachment trial resumes on November 9.
The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte has listed at least 24 initial witnesses it intends to present upon the resumption of the impeachment trial next week.

In a statement, Senate impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said the court received two formal manifestations with requests for subpoena duces tecum and ad testificandum filed by the defense on November 4, in compliance with the five-day notice directive, covering the hearings from November 9 to 13. —VAL, GMA News Online

articles.title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US mid-term election results?
articles.summary: BBC Verify examines whether US voters were influenced by the data centre boom - and the impact anti-AI sentiment could have on the industry.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondent

A US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.
BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.
What did the voter poll suggest?

The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.
The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.

This follows other recent Pew Research polling, external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.
The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.
However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered "crucial or major factors" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).
Did the AI backlash affect Senate races?
But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.

BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.
So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.

But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.
These proposals include:

items: temporary bans on construction
ending tax breaks
requirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costs
mandates to use unionised construction workers
stricter environmental and transparency safeguards
local rights to veto

blocks.text: What could the election results mean for the future of the AI boom?
The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI, external, including for data centre construction.

Official data, external shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.

Analysis by Columbia Business School, external suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.

Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".

Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Stargate Oracle AI data centre spans roughly four million square feet in Abilene, Texas

blocks.text: The Stargate Oracle AI data centre spans roughly four million square feet in Abilene, Texas
However, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.

She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".

Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.

Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.
OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday, external - one day after the midterm results.
Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett
