articles.title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
articles.summary: Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the village of Bédar this summer.

blocks.text: Families of Britons killed in Spain wildfires demand answers
ByNick Beake
Europe correspondent
Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.
Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.
Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.
"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.
He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.

The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.
The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.
The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.
Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.
"It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.
The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.
'Issue the damned alert!'
Michael Chard built his house in Bédar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."
On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Christine and Michael Chard are among the 15 people killed in July's deadly wildfire in the village of Bédar

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy of the Chard family
Christine and Michael Chard are among the 15 people killed in July's deadly wildfire in the village of Bédar

Duncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked.
"This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.
Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.
Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.
The families reject that.
"Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."
Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.

He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true.

"The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."

Bédar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.

blocks.caption: Satellite map of south-eastern Spain showing the area affected by a wildfire near Bédar, inland from the Mediterranean coast. Dark brown and black burn scars are highlighted within a boxed area around Bédar. Nearby towns marked on the map include Los Gallardos, Mojácar on the coast, and Palomares…

blocks.text: Of the 15 people who died in Bédar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.
In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".
Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze.
"The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.
He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future.
"They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."
'A huge hole in our lives'
Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.
They had lived in Bédar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church.
"They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."
She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave.
"They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.
Her parents died on the part of Bédar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.
Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.
Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.

But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.
Gillam-Kirton fears they were her father's remains.
Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.
Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Danni Gillam-Kirton says she found human bones and her parents' possessions in the burnt-out shell of their car

blocks.text: Image source, Danni Gillam-Kirton
Danni Gillam-Kirton says she found human bones and her parents' possessions in the burnt-out shell of their car
The fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.
But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower fire investigation, believe the fragments were human.
"We still don't know who or what they are," she said.

Gillam-Kirton complained to the Guardia Civil. She says the reply told her only that the matter had been passed to the courts, and offered condolences for "the death of your relative", in the singular, when in fact she had lost both her parents.
"It feels like they're going to hope that we exhaust ourselves," she said. "Either the burden of grief is going to be enough for us to give up, or that we're going to financially exhaust ourselves."
Gillam-Kirton says there is "a real lack of empathy when you're dealing with families that have lost so much".
The one thing she wants above all is for someone to acknowledge what went wrong: "No-one seems to be willing to say 'do you know what, we made a mistake and for that we are sorry'."
The death toll in Bédar was the highest from any single fire in Spain during the summer of 2026, and one of the largest in the country's history.
Many victims were trapped as they tried to escape the village, as survivor Malcolm Timbrell told me outside his devastated home in July.
The cause of the disaster, also known as the Los Gallardos fire after the neighbouring town where it started, is the subject of a criminal investigation.
In July, the Guardia Civil said it was believed to have been started by a fallen power line, but that explanation has been called into question.

The BBC has seen a letter in which the Andalusian government refused a request from Socialist MPs for its official reports on the fire. These included any documents explaining why no alert was sent to mobile phones.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pete (far left) and Fran (far right) both died in the wildfire in July. Karen (second left) wants to know more about what happened to them

blocks.text: Image source, Gillam family handout
Pete (far left) and Fran (far right) both died in the wildfire in July. Karen (second left) wants to know more about what happened to them
The letter, signed by Sanz in September, said the documents could not be released because the criminal investigation is under secreto de sumario, a court order keeping the case file confidential.

Gillam-Kirton says the criminal case is focused on how the fire started, and that it will not necessarily examine the emergency response unless families pay lawyers to put that evidence before the judge.
"How can you have faith in these measures that they're putting in to mitigate future disasters if you don't know fully what happened the first time around?" she said.
"That's why you have a public inquiry," said Duncan Chard, "because the public need answers."
Families in the UK, Belgium and Spain have set up various support groups, as well as a website called helpbedar.com.
They have launched an appeal to pay for legal action, aiming to raise €100,000 (£83,000). Fundraising events are being held in both Spain and the UK, and so far about €11,000 has been collected.
Relatives say their fight is like David and Goliath.
"We are getting steamrolled by the Andalusian government," said Chard.
Ultimately, the families say all they want is answers, and for lessons to be learned so that others do not suffer the same ordeal.
They say they want their fight to be a tribute to their loved ones who died.
"I feel like this is all I can do for them," said Gillam-Kirton.

articles.title: Minister tells energy suppliers to do more to help households tackle unpaid bills this winter
articles.summary:
Bosses from Great Britain’s biggest energy companies called to meeting as part of government’s debt relief plan

An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy…

blocks.text: An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.
Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.

The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.

The minister for energy consumers, Polly Billington, is understood to have told bosses from energy companies including Octopus Energy, British Gas and EDF Energy that suppliers would still need to play a “crucial role” in tackling the longstanding issue of problem debt alongside the government’s multibillion-pound support package.
Suppliers are expected to proactively identify customers who may be under financial strain and offer help such as debt payment plans or pointing them in the direction of debt advice services.

The government is also planning to work with the industry to make it easier to spot households that may need extra help, and to modernise payment systems to make it easier to pay. The government has backed the use of smart meters and smart pre-pay meters to help households track their spending and avoid getting into arrears.

blocks.caption: Polly Billington, the minister for energy consumers and Labour MP for East Thanet, said she knew ‘energy debt weighs heavily on millions of families across the country’. Photograph: Polly Braden/The Guardian

blocks.text: One attendee of the online roundtable meeting said there was “clearly a lot of ambition” behind the government’s plans, and the minister wanted to get the suppliers together with consumer groups “to make sure it is delivered”.

The meeting was attended by senior leaders from the largest six energy suppliers, and representatives from the industry trade association Energy UK, the fuel poverty charity National Energy Action, and five consumer advice groups including Citizens Advice.

In a statement after the meeting, Billington said: “I know that energy debt weighs heavily on millions of families across the country. That affects all of us, with the costs passed on to other billpayers.”
The average household currently pays about £50 a year on their energy bill to service unpaid energy bills across the market, but this would be likely to rise without action to shrink the debt pile.

The government believes that the one-off energy debt relief scheme, and new measures to keep debt from building up again in future, could save all households about £130 on average over the next 10 years.
after newsletter promotion

“That is exactly why we’re bringing in measures to help vulnerable households that have been in energy debt since the energy crisis a few years ago. Energy is an essential and making it affordable for everyone is our top priority,” said Billington.

Gillian Cooper, the director of energy at Citizens Advice, who attended the meeting, said that with typical annual energy bills predicted to increase again in January it was “essential” that the government’s new initiative “not only tackles existing energy debt, but also includes protections to help prevent households from falling into it in the first place”.

About 40% of unpaid bills are understood to build up during the process of moving home. The government plans to tackle this with reforms including a new obligation on landlords to provide meter readings and moving dates to their supplier when a tenant moves in or out of a property.

Rachel Fletcher, a director at Octopus Energy, the country’s biggest energy supplier, said she was “pleased to see a focus on improving what suppliers do to prevent customers from falling into debt in the first place”.
“Nothing in this package should weaken suppliers’ incentive to keep innovating and investing to help customers avoid and manage debt,” Fletcher said.

articles.title: Police turn to charities for help with teenagers caught up in online child abuse
articles.summary:
As new pornography laws come into force, officers say viewing extreme content could lead young people towards abuse images

Police forces are turning to specialist charities and partner…

blocks.text: Police forces are turning to specialist charities and partner agencies to cope with the growing number of teenagers caught up in online child abuse.
As new pornography laws come into force, frontline officers warn that young people are going down a pathway through extreme content that could lead to real-life abusive images of children.

From Friday, it will be illegal to publish or possess pornography showing strangulation, incest – including some step-relations – or adults acting out fantasies of sex with under-16s. The ban is built on years of campaigning that links pornography to real-life harm.

“This will be difficult to police,” said DC Sarah Turner, part of a team of specialist officers investigating child abuse in West Mercia. “Teen is one of the most popular porn terms; there is a huge appetite for this material, it leads to blurred lines.”
Police and legal experts say that while the new laws are urgently needed, the government must emphasise that they are aimed at large platforms rather than “what individuals have on their phone”.
DCI Gerard Smith, who leads the West Mercia team, told the Guardian: “There has to be a focus on the distributors in order to prevent the sharing of this material at source.”

Smith’s specialist officers see the impact of violent pornography daily as they knock on doors in the early hours to arrest individuals who are viewing or sharing child abuse material. “The volume of arrests is going up very significantly,” he said.
Across England and Wales every month, police arrest about 1,000 people – most of them men – for online child sexual abuse offences.

Turner said that on the dark web, offenders used sites that “resemble in style a regular porn site”. She added: “Dark web abuse sites are heavily linked to surface websites in style and content. The search terms may be similar, even the same. But the videos will be of real children being sexually abused.”
The officers say that men report having travelled through escalating extreme pornography habits to get to “a dark place”.

“They describe a numbness to extreme material,” said DC Pep Saladino. “There is a desensitisation – that is how they find themselves in a dark place. Often the men we arrest tell us they are glad to have been caught.”

The West Mercia officers, like others across the country, see so many young people – some in their early teens – in their work that they are looking at a pilot scheme that would send civilians to visit children who are viewing illegal material.
Some of this is sexting between teenagers; some involves teenagers being exposed to violent images of child abuse through chat sites and forums.

“Several forces are looking at this following a successful project in Surrey called Solah,” said Smith. “We don’t want to criminalise children, so if there are no aggravating factors like they are coercing others, then the police are not the best agency to provide safeguarding advice.”
The officers are clear that many of the men they meet have spiralled towards child abuse from pornography.

“We see many young adults who started out watching pornography as children,” said DS Peter Wheeler. “They have escalated down the rabbit hole. Ultimately, we have to look at the big porn platforms. These are multimillion-pound companies.”
New adverts from the Ministry of Justice have been circulating on social media warning extreme pornography users to “delete it” before 6 November or face prison sentences of up to five years.

Clare McGlynn, a professor of law at Durham University and an expert on the legal regulation of pornography, wants to see the government make clear that the law was about cleaning up pornography sites.
She said: “I am concerned about misinformation online that this law is about policing what individuals have on their phones. It’s not. This is about platforms removing very egregious content.

“We are talking about the normalisation of strangulation, the normalisation of incest, of videos with girls in pigtails with teddy bears, of adults acting out child abuse and that extreme content being pushed by algorithms to the public for profit by porn platforms.”
McGlynn said social media was also an issue: “You can look up horrific material on X. What will they be doing about it tomorrow?”

A report by the Conservative peer Gabby Bertin sparked the new law. It called for a new regulatory body to oversee the pornography industry. McGlynn said the job could go to the British Board of Film Classification, adding: “Ofcom need to tell us when they will start enforcing these laws. So far they are a lethargic regulator.”
A spokesperson for Ofcom said the watchdog had to consult on any changes to its guidance and codes for platforms.

They added: “New legal duties on tech companies to deal with this content will come into force once we have updated our codes of practice and guidance – as required by law – and we’re preparing to consult on this in the first half of 2027.

“We’re already engaging with platforms to make sure they’re preparing to comply, and once in force, we’ll be holding them to account. In the first 18 months of the Online Safety Act coming into force, we’ve investigated more than 100 platforms, and issued fines totalling more than £7m against 11 providers.”
Vicky Young of the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, which runs a helpline to encourage people to stop viewing child abuse images, welcomed the ban.

She said: “We’ve been raising concerns about extreme pornography for a long time. Thousands of people who contact our Stop It Now helpline tell us that extreme pornography has played a role in their pathway to viewing illegal sexual images of children. We’re pleased to see this ban because it will make children safer.”

articles.title: We should read more slice-of-life books
articles.summary: Satoshi Yagisawa has a way of capturing the intimacy of the mundane

blocks.text: Satoshi Yagisawa has a way of capturing the intimacy of the mundane

items: The text discusses the overwhelming nature of modern life and the importance of unplugging, particularly through engaging with slice-of-life literature.
Satoshi Yagisawa's books, such as 'Days at the Morisaki Bookshop,' provide relatable characters and settings that foster a sense of community and emotional connection.
These narratives emphasize the beauty of ordinary experiences and the healing power of taking time to appreciate life's simple moments.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

It’s easy to be overwhelmed with problems that we feel like are out of our control, especially when you’re endlessly scrolling online. Political dynasties seemingly playing the role of Game of Thrones characters, tech bros running amok with AI, and social media deregulating our emotional stability.

I’ve built routines to help me unplug and spend time off my screen, and one effective way I found was to dive deep into slice-of-life books. These are books that highlight ordinary people going through somewhat normal situations, but with the kind of deep intimacy that you can only get from being in the moment and being able to practice the art of noticing (in a way, like street photography).

There are lots of amazing slice-of-life books that talk about life in interesting ways. The “Kamogawa Food Detectives” by Hisashi Kashiwai, for example, uses memories around food. “Heartstopper” by Alice Oseman is a coming-of-age story that relies on quiet vignettes instead of big plot twists to drive the narrative.

Three books that I’ve read, then read again, then read once more are works by Japanese author Satoshi Yagisawa. Namely, these are “Days at the Morisaki Bookshop,” its sequel “More Days at the Morisaki Bookshop,” and “Days at the Torunka Cafe.” They’re all cozy reads, and I love bringing any one of these with me to a coffee shop and spending time with them while listening to jazz music.

And what I especially love about these books is how easy it is to see myself in any of the characters in them as well as the soft energy that comes from how the stories are all grounded in spaces that are shared by small and tight-knit communities.

“Days at the Morisaki Bookshop” and its sequel are mostly set in Jimbocho, a famous neighborhood in Chiyoda, Tokyo, Japan, known as the largest secondhand and antiquarian book town that has about 200 bookstores. “Days at the Torunka Cafe,” on the other hand, is set in a fictional neighborhood in Tokyo. The Torunka Cafe itself is said to be tucked away in a narrow alleyway that some discovered after following a mysterious cat to the place.

These locations serve as third places that anchor the characters, and are written with such gentle detail that it’s as if they actually exist in real life. The Morisaki Bookshop was a building filled to the brim with old books, had a musty smell, and was prone to humidity. Torunka Cafe was filled with the aroma of fresh coffee, a respite people frequented after long walks, and a place that held so much history.
They’re also witnesses to how the characters live and the challenges they face, as well as both big and quiet wins that they gain.

And in all honesty, I crave these kinds of third spaces and yearn for that sense of community that comes with meeting people there. Life can seem fragmented at times, and it’s amazing to witness how an unassuming cafe or bookshop can keep a mesh of people connected.

The characters that Satoshi Yagisawa writes feel real, not just because they’re of ordinary people, but also because they make the same decisions that we would if we were in their situation. No one is a superhero or a villain in these stories. They’re going through love, grief, regret, and great joy just as we do.
Takako in “Days at the Morisaki Bookshop” experiences an unusual “breakup” from a situationship she thought was getting serious and finds herself moving across town just to get away from it all.

She was called “Sleep Monster” by a regular who noticed all she did was stay in bed when she first moved to Jimbocho. But eventually, she starts building up a routine that includes clearing up the bookshop her uncle inherited, finding books that she enjoys, and discovering a coffee shop to read them in, as well as making new friends who pull her out of her own head.
Takako’s healing was messy and slow to start, but her journey was comforting to read because it felt familiar. Satoshi Yagisawa articulated the flurry of emotions we go through.
Here’s an excerpt that I wrote in my own commonplace journal (where I place things I read or hear that I want to remember) about Takako’s story:

“There’s a whimsy and contemplativeness in Takako that I connect with – how she allows life to whisk her away is a quality I wish I had. But she’s also able to steel herself and sit still – a quality I see in us both.”

Ultimately, Yagisawa’s books are a quiet rebellion against a world that demands constant optimization and rapid-fire emotional processing. They remind us that we don’t always need a grand, world-saving tale to pull us out of a slump or distract us from doomscrolling.
Sometimes, the most profound thing we can do is perhaps take space in a cramped room smelling of old paper, or allow our whimsy to take us to a narrow alleyway cafe and try a new drink.
These slice-of-life books allow us a chance to, well, experience life outside our phones! They become opportunities to pull up a chair somewhere, feel the cold air, and read the world. – Rappler.com

The 69-year-old was convicted of several offences including "subversion against the political power of the State".
What were the charges against Au Kam San?
Au was accused of providing false information to anti-China organizations outside Macau to incite hatred against the city's government and Beijing.
The teacher-turned-lawmaker was detained in July 2025, in what was the first publicly known prosecution under Macau's national security law since it was implemented in 2009.

Au "personally provided, over a long period of time, assistance and collaboration to external hostile organisations in the collection, preparation, and public dissemination of various images and information that were manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the political authority of the State," a court statement said.

The court added that Au also sought to "incite hatred among Macau residents against the Central People's Government, with the intent to overthrow and undermine the fundamental system of the State enshrined in the Constitution of the People's Republic of China."
What have critics said about Au's trial?
Au's closed-door trial — which ended in September in three days — had raised concerns about fairness.
An open trial was ruled out by a judge to safeguard national security interests, the court had said earlier.
Critics say that Au's case illustrates China's emphasis on security and its intolerance of dissent, even though Macau's pro-democracy movement has never been as influential as its neighbor Hong Kong.
Last year, the European Uniondenounced Au's arrest, saying it added to the concerns about the "erosion of political pluralism" in Macau.
Au served in Macau's legislature dominated by pro-China loyalists for two decades and stepped down in 2021.
He co-organized Macau's vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
Macau is a former Portuguese colony which reverted to China in 1999. Like Hong Kong, it operates as a special administrative region of China.

articles.title: Australia faces same issues that flipped control of US Congress in midterms, experts say
articles.summary:
Anthony Albanese’s government has taken a blow due to Iran war but voter anxiety around cost of living and datacentres may hit harder

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Democrats’ stunning midterm victory should broaden Australia’s alliance with the US, observers say, even as a new power base emerges in Washington, affecting Aukus, datacentre development and relations with China.

Cabinet ministers, diplomats and Australia’s defence industrial sector closely watched the results this week, with control of the US Congress flipping to the Democrats and the outlook for Donald Trump’s final two years in office badly dinted.

Public fury over rising living costs, particularly fuel prices, and the impact of datacentres, were also two factors in the midterms results that carry warnings for the Australian government, analysts said.
Bruce Wolpe, a senior fellow at the United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s ability to rile up voters had been undermined by cost of living.
Wolpe said the Albanese government was taking a hit because of the economic fallout from the Iran war.
“I think a lot of people are wondering what does this [Australian] government do?” he said. “Have they lost control of the economy?
“In January, before the Iran war, the outlook looked pretty good. But now, after going through a budget process and the war … people are just very uncertain as to where this is going to end up.
“It is not an immediately solvable problem, and people really dislike it.”
Westpac’s head of international economics, Elliot Clarke, said the landslide midterms results had “dramatically changed” the outlook for the Iran war, which could affect the economy in Australia.
“It has changed the ‘atmospherics’ around the Middle East conflict,” he said. “It’s positive news.”

blocks.caption: Donald Trump claimed that Republicans had fared poorly in the midterms because he was not on the ballot. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP

blocks.text: There was a steep drop in the global oil price as the election results filtered out. The Brent crude benchmark, which had threatened to pass its April peak, has instead plunged by 20%.
More confidence in a potential resolution in the Middle East would also help curb inflation and help central banks hold back on rate hikes, according to Clarke.
“It definitely changes the calculus,” he said.
Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie said the results showed economic messaging was critical.

“People feel worse off after tariffs and after the war in Iran, and Donald Trump has said a few times now that he doesn’t really care,” he told 2GB. “Our job is always to deliver better outcomes for the Australian people.”
The future of the alliance

Arthur Sinodinos, a former ambassador to Washington, said the change on Capitol Hill was a chance for Australian officials to progress policy goals with both US parties, and to consider the relationship beyond the 2028 presidential election.

“The main question mark is: ‘What is the impact on geopolitics across the world?’” he said. “Does this inject more uncertainty into American foreign policy? We’ve already had a lot of volatility in that regard.”
“The Congress may put more pressure on the administration to support Ukraine and pass measures that involve funding munitions to Ukraine.

“I think the Chinese will feel more emboldened, but I don’t think that translates into some sudden action on Taiwan. Trump has made it clear in the past that they won’t do anything on his watch, and I think he would feel bound to act if they did.”
Sinodinos praised prime minister Anthony Albanese’s professional approach to dealing with the often unconventional US president.
“I think the Australian government’s reaction after this vote is keep working with the administration, keep their heads down,” he said.

Trump claimed that Republicans had fared poorly because he was not on the ballot, despite repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot. The vice-president, JD Vance, called Trump’s war in Iran “the obvious culprit”.
Ed Husic, former industry minister, wants a radical shake up in the alliance.
“The moment to reset the relationship with the Trump administration is right now,” he said.
“A completely different Congress will require that administration to do things differently, including not hurting allies – friends, such as Australia – with tariffs.”
Abe Denmark, a partner at The Asia Group and an architect of the Aukus agreement in the Biden administration, warned against over-interpreting the results for Australia.
“What will change is how power is distributed in Washington,” he said.

“There will now be new centres of power to engage: Democratic chairs controlling authorisations and appropriations, Republicans more willing to break ranks, and 2028 hopefuls from both parties looking to stand out.

“While this gives Australia more points to engage, it also generates more noise. The challenge for Canberra, as with all allies and partners, will be to differentiate political positioning from durable policy.”
Denmark said the Democrats could take a different view from Trump on Aukus spending, as the US submarine industrial base needs a dramatic step up in production.
He said a government funding deal and passage of a key defence spending bill were urgent priorities for Congress.
A warning on datacentres

Husic also flagged possible changes to the US’s approach to AI regulation, and a flow on effect as the Albanese government prepare major legislation for 2027. Vermont senator Bernie Sanders has already called for a moratorium on new construction, warning that voters wanted the environment and humanity itself protected.
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said it was no coincidence that datacentre hotspots like Texas, Georgia and Ohio had shifted to support Democrats.

“Communities are being asked to hand over their land, water and power to some of the world’s wealthiest tech companies, yet the benefits for ordinary Australians remain remarkable difficult to identify,” she said.
The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, observed cost-of-living and datacentre anxiety was at play in both countries.

“What we are very mindful about here is that you’ve got to get the social licence right in respect of datacentres – where they’re built, and the place where they shouldn’t be built is in suburbs – and also making sure that the right power and the right water is brought to these datacentres,” he said.

articles.title: VP Sara to visit Hong Kong ahead of impeachment trial resumption
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President announced that Vice President Sara Duterte will be in Hong Kong until November 8, just one day before the resumption of her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: November 6, 2026 | 12:15pm
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte (front R) leaves court after posting bail in Quezon City, suburban Manila on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Vice President (OVP) announced on Friday, November 6, that Vice President Sara Duterte will be in Hong Kong until November 8, just one day before the resumption of her impeachment trial.
The office specified that Duterte would cover all travel costs using personal funds. No government money, resources or facilities would be used for the trip.
The OVP also confirmed that Duterte was granted permission to travel by the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98, which issued an arrest warrant for the vice president in September.

The warrant, stemming from grave threats made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, was among the allegations included in the four original articles of impeachment against Duterte.
The impeachment trial is set to resume on Monday, November 9, despite a pending Supreme Court challenge regarding the voting threshold to convict the vice president.
During the sessions, the defense will present its evidence under a narrower case that retains only Article II of the impeachment complaint, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth.

Duterte's lawyers submitted a 25-person witness lineup for the hearings from November 9 to 13. The defense's first planned witness, Ralph Sarmiento, a former law dean at the University of St. La Salle in Bacolod City, has declined to take the stand.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's manager moves to drop complaint against late singer's nephew
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's longtime manager moved Thursday to drop a complaint that accused the late singer's nephew who acted as her head of security with threatening her estate and its employees.

image.caption: Dolly Parton's longtime manager, Danny Nozell, seen here in 2014 with Parton, has moved to drop a complaint against the late singer's nephew. (Rick Diamond/Getty Images for Webster PR)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Dolly Parton's longtime manager moved Thursday to drop a complaint that accused the late singer's nephew who acted as her head of security with threatening her estate and its employees.
Danny Nozell had secured a restraining order against Bryan Seaver, saying he threatened his aunt's estate

The proposed dismissal and apparent settlement brought a sudden, unexpected and unexplained end to an ugly rift in the beloved country superstar's inner circle that began while she was sick with cancer and spilled into public view in the weeks after her Aug. 25 death.

The manager, Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, an entity founded to manage and protect Parton's estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September. Nozell was seeking to turn the order into a permanent injunction against Seaver.

A very brief filing in a Tennessee court Thursday gives no reason why the complaint is being withdrawn. It says only that a proposed order was being drafted for the judge's approval to dismiss the case without prejudice, meaning it can be refiled again. A court filing from a day earlier said the two sides had reached an agreement, but that gave no details either.
The fight was about to become even more public with the first hearing on the matter that was slated for Tuesday, with the two sides set to argue over the proposed permanent injunction.
The Associated Press sent emails seeking comment from lawyers for She's Alive, Seaver and his company.

items: Dolly Parton's estate has filed a lawsuit against her nephew. Here's what's happened so far

blocks.text: She's Alive terminated Seaver and SAPS in early September, and the following week petitioned for the restraining order against him, arguing that his "terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable."

The petition said that starting shortly before Parton's death and continuing after, Seaver made threats and aimed them directly at She's Alive's "personnel, counsel, and business partners. In writing, he vowed to ‘destroy the entire brand.'"
It says he "called himself ‘literally an international arms dealer and mercenary,'" and said everyone "needs to be worried about what I might do."
In granting the temporary order, Chancellor I'Ashea L. Myles cited Seaver's "claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate."
Dolly Parton's trailblazing influence and songwriting legacy

Parton was a widely adored singer, songwriter, philanthropist and country music icon who rose from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to a stardom that spanned generations with songs including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You.
She also left behind a business empire, much of it based in her hometown, that employed many of her close friends and family.

articles.title: Court orders jail authorities to submit detailed report on Romualdez's whereabouts
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to submit a detailed report on the whereabouts of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez since…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 12:06pm

The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to submit a detailed report on the whereabouts of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez since the lawmaker’s detention in New Quezon City jail in Payatas last September.

The anti-graft court issued the order on November 5 in light of the allegations of columnist Ramon Tulfo that Romualdez, who is facing a P7.4 billion plunder case over his alleged involvement in the flood control scam, has been going in and out of his detention as he pleases.
Tulfo has since retracted his report, saying a source provided him false information.

“Considering the materiality of the allegations in the aforementioned Facebook post which raise concerns on the court's effective custody over accused Romualdez, the BJMP QC Jail - Male Dormitory, through Jail Superintendent [Lourdes] Pacion, is ordered to examine all CCTV footage from the time of accused Romualdez's transfer to the facility on September 14, 2026, up to yesterday, November 4, 2026 and to submit a notarized report detailing the whereabouts of accused Romualdez per the CCTV surveillance system,” the anti-graft court said.

The report, the anti-graft court said, should include specific places where accused Romualdez was and is confined since his detention, as well as the common areas used by the lawmaker which covers the following:

items: CCTV surveillance system operating logs, system status reports, and maintenance records.
Records identifying the persons authorized to operate, control, maintain, disable, or restore the CCTV system.
CCTV system's access logs, audit trails, and records of any deletion, alteration, copying, or retrieval of CCTV recordings.
Records of power interruptions in the BJMP QC Jail - Male Dormitory, indicating therein how long the power interruption lasted, if any, and what remedies were taken.
Operating logs of BJMP QC Jail - Male Dormitory's backup power supply.

Vehicle entry and exit logbooks, gate pass records, and/or vehicle movement registers; Records of BJMP QC Jail - Male Dormitory's ambulance use, indicating therein the exact departure time, driver's name, medical report, destination, PDL concerned, and other passengers; and roster of jail guards, gatekeepers, medical staff on shift, indicating therein the specific post they assumed, as well as the names of persons allowed to assist Romualdez and stay with him in the facility.
Latest medical report of accused Romualdez, including information of any medical examination conducted upon accused Romualdez inside and outside the facility.

blocks.text: In addition, the Sandiganbayan said the report must state the inadequacies of the CCTV surveillance system as told by Pacion before the anti-graft court on November 5 for the updates.

Further, the Sandiganbayan ordered Jail Superintendent Pacion and Dr. Henry Fabro, as well as the IT personnel of the BJMP QC Jail - Male Dormitory to appear on November 9, 2026, at 8:30 in the morning for another hearing.
Pacion earlier told the anti-graft court that Romualdez has a personal staff with his cell to attend to his daily needs amid an unstable mental health condition.
Pacion, however, stressed that Romualdez has never left the detention premises. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: NBI to file estafa, waste management raps vs. pet crematorium operators; seeks ILBO
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is set to file complaints against individuals allegedly involved in the improper disposal of pet remains in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 12:00pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is set to file complaints against individuals allegedly involved in the improper disposal of pet remains in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag on Friday said the agency's Environmental Crime Division (ENCD) has completed preparing the complaints and would submit them to the Department of Justice (DOJ).
"This morning, natapos na ng ating ENCD ang pagpapaghanda doon sa kasong ifa-file. And this morning, they will be going to the Department of Justice (DOJ) to file the charges," Matibag said.
The complaints involve alleged estafa and violations of the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act. The NBI is also looking into possible violations of the Consumer Act of the Philippines.

Matibag said five of the 25 complainants already completed their paperwork with the NBI. Other individuals reportedly filed their complaints with the Philippine National Police (PNP) in Bacoor, Cavite.
The NBI is also seeking an Immigration Lookout Bulletin Order (ILBO) against three individuals under investigation in connection with the case.
In a letter dated November 5 and addressed to Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, the NBI requested an ILBO against three individuals.

They are being investigated over the discovery of 25 animal remains, consisting of three cats and 22 dogs, inside plastic bags and sacks in a vacant lot in Barangay Minuyan Proper, San Jose del Monte.
Initial investigation showed that some of the animal remains bore identification tags and weight markings reportedly traceable to a pet crematorium operated or managed by the individuals.

The NBI said the requested ILBO would allow the Bureau of Immigration (BI) to monitor and record the individuals' international travel movements to ensure their availability amid probe and possible legal proceedings.
Matibag said the alleged scheme involved a pet crematorium in Bacoor that had supposedly arranged for another facility in Bulacan to handle the cremation of animals.
The arrangement allegedly stemmed from the failure of a couple to deliver a cremation machine to the Bacoor facility despite receiving partial payment.
The Bacoor operator supposedly agreed to send the pet remains to the couple's facility in Bulacan for cremation.
However, as the volume of remains increased, the couple allegedly contracted individuals to dispose of the animals instead of cremating them.
"Kaya kung maalala niyo, tatlong sites 'yung pinagdalhan niyan. So 'yun 'yung mga sites kung saan-saan na instead binaon 'yung mga supposed to be na-crinemate na mga pets," he said.
(So if you remember, there were three sites where the remains were dumped. So those are the sites where the remains, which were supposed to be buried, were dumped instead of being buried.)
Matibag said both the Bacoor and Bulacan parties appeared to have liabilities as investigators believe both sides knew about and agreed to the arrangement.
The NBI is also looking into how the establishments obtained occupancy and business permits despite allegedly lacking the necessary equipment to operate a pet crematorium.
Matibag said the agency would ask the concerned local government units to explain how the permits were issued. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: AI sharpens cat-and-mouse hacking battle as companies strengthen defenses
articles.summary: Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an…

blocks.text: AI. 'AI Artificial Intelligence' words, a keyboard and a robotics hand in this illustration taken, September 23, 2026
Dado Ruvic/Reuters

Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an international registry of disclosed security flaws

items: Companies worldwide are facing an increase in cyber threats, with AI making attacks more sophisticated and frequent, leading to significant financial losses and operational disruptions.
In response to the surge in vulnerabilities, organizations are investing in AI-powered security tools to enhance their defenses and manage the growing workload on IT departments.

The rapid evolution of cyber threats, including high-profile attacks on supermarkets and cryptocurrency exchanges, underscores the urgent need for improved cybersecurity measures and the adoption of AI technologies.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

From hacked supermarket fridges and a record cryptocurrency theft at Binance to an emergency over flaws in widely used web software, companies worldwide are facing a wave of cyber threats executives say AI is accelerating and making more sophisticated.

The surge is straining IT departments, with staff working overnight to patch software vulnerabilities, prompting some companies to turn to and increase investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the workload.

A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks in which hackers raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures, forcing retailers to discard millions of dollars’ worth of spoiled food, underscored the urgency.
“It’s a never-ending game of cat and mouse, with very high stakes,” said Marnie Wilking, chief security officer at travel platform Booking.com.

“We shut down one route, and before we’ve even finished rolling out the fix, the bad guys have moved on to the next,” she said, adding that hundreds of engineers at the company were now building AI-powered defense systems.

Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an international registry of disclosed security flaws.

“We’re seeing events of a magnitude every week, or even every couple of days, that used to be months apart,” Markus Noga, chief technology officer of German web hosting company Ionos, which serves seven million customers, told Reuters.

Ionos said it changed its security practices after seeing a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring systems to scan for threats and using AI-assisted tools to install patches on its systems around the clock.
“I’m kind of limited to what a nine-to-five office hours team can do and that’s no longer good enough,” Noga said.

Binance, hit by hackers who stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency, said it would increase investment in AI-enhanced detection systems. The Port of Rotterdam is working on an AI-powered “cyber shield,” while Siemens is testing advanced AI models for defensive security.

Dutch-based grocer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Stop & Shop and Giant Food chains in the US, was hit by two hacks in the past month. The first, in mid-October, led to more than €200 million ($225 million) in sales losses and prompted a profit warning.

In that incident, Ahold took its websites and apps offline for a week after detecting an intrusion. This week, some of its stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were among those hit by cyberattacks on refrigerators across a dozen European countries.
“We’re adjusting to a new reality,” CFO Jolanda Poots-Bijl told Reuters, adding smaller firms were particularly exposed. At the same time, AI is a defensive tool, she said.
“AI also helps us to detect and to restore in a much faster way than we were ever able to do in the past,” she added.
McKinsey projects the global market for cybersecurity products and services sold by outside vendors will grow from $223 billion in 2025 to $346 billion by 2029.

The refrigerator cyberattacks show how AI is putting pressure on companies to patch systems quickly once a vulnerability is found, said Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer at cybersecurity firm Claroty.
Claroty published research in August, months before the attacks began, outlining weaknesses in refrigeration controllers.

After a first wave of attacks hit stores in France on October 11, Claroty researchers used widely available AI tools to reproduce the flaws and take control of a test device, highlighting the risk of further attacks.
“We were able to recreate it for six dollars and 28 minutes,” Tufts said.

The October 21 disclosure of two AI-discovered flaws in the PHP programming language, which underpins many websites, prompted governments and companies from Tokyo to Helsinki to take websites offline as a precaution.

US internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare reported that attempts to exploit PHP flaws rose from thousands to millions within hours of their disclosure. AI-discovered bugs could lead to more disruption in future, it told Reuters.
“The threat is real, it’s growing,” said Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane, adding cybersecurity was “more important today than it was yesterday and will be even more important tomorrow”.

At Swiss building materials maker Holcim, which took its website offline around 9:30 p.m. (1930 GMT) on October 21 to install PHP fixes and restore service before midnight, Chief Financial Officer Steffen Kindler echoed those comments.
“We need to get smarter. Both sides are heavily equipped,” he said. “Both sides use AI, and that race is continuing.” – Rappler.com

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. administered Friday the oath of office to 10 of his ad interim appointees heading various government agencies.
In a ceremony at Malacañan Palace, the following Cabinet officials took their oath before the President:

items: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto
Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida
Public Works Secretary Giovanni Lopez
Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino
Health Secretary Edwin Mercado
Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna
Tourism Secretary Maria Bernardita Mathay
Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon
Budget Secretary Kim Robert De Leon
Philippine Space Agency Director General Gay Jane Perez

blocks.text: In an interview, Recto explained that the oath-taking signifies that the Cabinet officials have received ad interim appointments from the President and are now set to face the powerful Commission on Appointments (CA).

“Itong oath-taking ngayon ay ibig sabihin lahat kami dito ngayon, ad interim appointments ng Pangulo. Dadaan kaming lahat sa Commission on Appointments. Nakapag-submit na tayo sa Commission on Appointments,” Recto said.

(This oath-taking today means that all of us here have received ad interim appointments from the President. We will all go through the Commission on Appointments. We have already submitted our appointments to the Commission on Appointments.)
The CA is mandated to approve or disapprove appointments made by the President of the Philippines, the confirmation of which is required under the 1987 Constitution.

The commission’s function “forms part of the very delicate mechanism of checks and balances established by the Constitution to ensure that the coordinate departments of the government will function in a way that will be most conducive to the public welfare,” based on its website. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Hong Kong’s Joshua Wong: From teenage protest leader to a decade behind bars
articles.summary: He will be approaching 40 when he leaves jail, a long way off from his days as a one-year-old toddler in 1997, when Britain handed his city back to China with a promise of extensive autonomy and…

blocks.text: DEMOCRACY ACTIVISTS. File photo shows pro-democracy activists Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow arrive at the Eastern Court by police van after being arrested on suspicion for organizing illegal protests, in Hong Kong, China August 30, 2019.
Tyrone Siu/REUTERS

He will be approaching 40 when he leaves jail, a long way off from his days as a one-year-old toddler in 1997, when Britain handed his city back to China with a promise of extensive autonomy and freedom of speech and assembly

items: Joshua Wong, a prominent Hong Kong democracy activist and leader of the 2014 Umbrella Movement, was sentenced to an additional 10 years in prison for collusion with foreign entities under the national security law.
Wong began his activism at age 14 and became an international symbol of the pro-democracy movement, facing multiple incarcerations for his dissent against the Chinese government.

Despite his guilty plea, Wong maintained that he believed his actions were lawful and expressed a desire for Hong Kong's future, emphasizing his commitment to the democracy movement even while in prison.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

HONG KONG – Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong, once a leader of the 2014 Umbrella Movement that posed one of the boldest populist challenges to the leaders of China’s Communist Party in decades, was sentenced on Thursday, November 5, to 10 more years in jail.
Wong, who has been behind bars since 2020, pleaded guilty to a charge of collusion with foreign entities under the Asian financial hub’s national security law, ushered in that year.

He will be approaching 40 when he leaves jail, a long way off from his days as a one-year-old toddler in 1997, when Britain handed his city back to China with a promise of extensive autonomy and freedom of speech and assembly.
“One national security officer said he and I were ‘enemies’ and lamented that he had lost many friends because of me,” Wong said on Thursday, recalling the day he was charged.
“I replied: ‘You are not my enemy. We are all Hong Kongers; there is no antagonism between us,'” he added in his mitigation comments.

Wong’s activist journey started at just 14, as he emerged on Hong Kong’s democratic stage by co-founding a group called Scholarism that held mass protests and ultimately forced the government to shelve plans for a pro-China national education scheme in schools.

By age 17, as a thin youth with bowl-cut hair and dark-rimmed glasses, Wong was the international face of the pro-democracy “Umbrella Movement,” referring to how protesters warded off riot police volleys of tear gas and pepper spray.

Wong’s activism and vocal dissent landed him in jail numerous times, not least after the Umbrella Movement drew hundreds of thousands of protesters at its peak to paralyze streets in the city’s heart for 79 days.
Prosecutors in the latest case accused Wong of working along with others to solicit foreign sanctions or hostile actions against Hong Kong and China between July and November 2020.
Though he pleaded guilty to the charge, Wong said he mistakenly thought his actions were within the law, adding that he had never advocated Hong Kong independence nor the collapse of China.
The timeframe of the events is key, since Beijing in late June of that year had imposed the National Security Law on the city following months of sometimes-violent pro-democracy protests in 2019.
The law effectively outlawed or put at risk many of the political activities that Wong and his peers once took for granted.

Wong became a familiar face on the international scene and a thorn in the side of authorities in Beijing and Hong Kong, featuring on the front cover of Time magazine in 2014 and in a Netflix documentary in 2017 that chronicled his political life.
Along with other Hong Kong critics of mainland China, including media tycoon Jimmy Lai, he was repeatedly nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

He made it a mission to drum up support for Hong Kong’s democracy movement at home and overseas, meeting politicians from the United States and Europe, drawing the wrath of Beijing, which called him a “black hand” of foreign forces.
Outsiders who met him during this time recall his striking air of quiet determination, and apparently unshakable convictions.
When Wong left jail in June 2019 at the height of the protests, he was not a leading figure in organizing the rallies, but he once again became one of the movement’s most globally recognized faces.

Scholarism had morphed into Demosisto, a political party that once backed a referendum on Hong Kong’s sovereignty and installed the youngest candidate ever on the city’s Legislative Council before he was disqualified.
Demosisto was disbanded within hours after the National Security Law was passed.
In 2017, just before another sentencing, Wong told more than 100 supporters who thronged the court lobby, some weeping, that he had no regrets.

“I hope Hong Kong people won’t give up,” he said. “Victory is ours. When we are released next year I hope we can see a Hong Kong that is full of hope. I want to see Hong Kong people not giving up. This is my last wish before I go to jail.”
Nearly 10 years on, Wong’s extended term in prison is the latest blow for a movement whose followers find themselves in detention, exile or, in the case of some, cowed into silence.

Standing in the dock on Thursday, Wong was silent as the judge sentenced him to 10 years in jail that will keep him in prison after his current term ends in January. The sentence will be served concurrently, effectively shortening it by two months.
Wong mentioned a desire to eventually look after his ageing parents above all.

This, along with the fact that books on Chinese history and Hong Kong’s mini-constitution were among the hundreds he was reading in jail, prompted the judge to hail Wong’s efforts at rehabilitation as “commendable.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Hegseth defends record as Pengaton chief, slams 'sham' push for his impeachment
articles.summary: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as "courageous and historic" after voters punished…

image.caption: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him. (Jam Sta Rosa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as "courageous and historic" after voters punished Republicans over it in this week’s midterm elections.
The Secretary of War issued a video message Thursday vowing to fight efforts to impeach him

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as "courageous and historic" after voters punished Republicans over it in this week's midterm elections.

Hegseth's remarks, posted ‌on social media, came as taunts from his foes in Congress intensified and U.S. President Donald Trump swatted away questions about whether he might fire Hegseth. Trump has commended his Pentagon chief.
The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, asked in a post: "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?"

Hegseth, a former Fox News host, has been a polarizing figure who has made enemies even within his own Republican Party. Critics in Congress are targeting his conduct ​of the Iran war, which U.S. Vice President JD Vance has said cost Republicans control of Congress, ​his firing of top military officers and strained relations with lawmakers as the administration seeks a $1.5-trillion US defence spending package.
Calls to investigate Hegseth

Democrats, who won control of Congress in Tuesday's elections, have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and congressional aides say that would include the ​firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, among other issues.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie promised to reintroduce articles of impeachment ⁠against Hegseth next week, warning that impeachment would ⁠be "much gentler" than what's in store for him once Republicans cede control of Congress next year ‌to Democrats.
"They'll have hearings & trials," Massie wrote on X.

items: JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

blocks.text: Hegseth defended his stewardship of the Pentagon in a more than four-minute video that boasted about firing senior Pentagon leaders, ending diversity initiatives and banning transgender individuals from the military.
"You see, they attack me — they attack us — because we are effective. It's not going to work. We will not back down," Hegseth said to the camera.
Impeachment 'didn't work' against Trump: Hegeseth
Calling the impeachment effort a "sham," Hegseth said that Trump himself was impeached ⁠twice.
Combative Hegseth defends Iran war strategy, Trump's mental state
"It's all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that," he said.

Trump on Thursday praised Hegseth when asked whether he expected any staffing changes, saying his defence secretary had "done a fantastic job" and suggesting that the opposition to him was tied to his firing ‌of generals.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday praised Hegseth when asked whether he expected any staffing changes, saying his defence secretary had 'done a fantastic job.' (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

"We had so many generals. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it. And many of those people were woke. I don't like a woke general. And so, he probably has opposition," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Trump also praised Hegseth's role in U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran.
"Venezuela has been unbelievable ... and in Iran, we are there for seven months and we control everything that we've wanted to control," he ​said.
Could be 'on chopping block'
Sources have said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their election losses.

On Wednesday, Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress, in extraordinary remarks ⁠that raised questions about whether Trump might still go ahead with a threatened resumption of major combat operations against Iran.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress in the recent U.S. midterm elections. (Tom Brenner/The Associated Press)
One Trump adviser said Hegseth "could be on the chopping block" ⁠because of the Iran war.
The War Department has said Hegseth is "100 per cent committed" to leading the Pentagon until the end of Trump's term.
Hegseth appealed to "patriotic" lawmakers to ⁠pass a ⁠funding request that aims to help the Pentagon pay for the ​Iran war and other spending priorities.

"Regardless of how people feel about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets nuclear weapons, ​we need to continue, as President Trump did in ⁠his first term, to rebuild our military," Hegseth said.
Hegseth faces 'a reckoning': senator

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis told CBS news on Tuesday night that Hegseth has "a reckoning" coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration's push for a $1.5-trillion US defence spending package in Congress.

Hegseth could also face scrutiny from Democrats over his Ukraine policy and U.S. military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes.

Representative Adam Smith, the Democrat who is expected to lead the House Armed Services Committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything ⁠from the Iran war to what he called the ‌erosion of the "apolitical foundation of the armed forces."

blocks.text: A woman who was shot during the Bondi beach terror attack has died in hospital almost 12 months after the massacre.
The 90-year-old woman had been in and out of hospital this year for treatment of injuries sustained during the attack on 14 December, a senior Jewish community source said on Friday.
The elderly woman had recently returned to hospital after developing an infection, where she died after having a stroke, the source said.
Her funeral was scheduled to take place on Monday. A family spokeperson requested “privacy during this difficult time”.
Fifteen people died after Naveed Akram, 24, and his father, 50-year-old Sajid Akram, opened fire at the Hanukkah festival at Bondi beach on 14 December last year. Forty people were injured.

articles.title: PCG responds to oil spill off Mariveles, Bataan
articles.summary: About 25 liters of used oil spilled into the coastal waters of Mariveles, Bataan, on Thursday, November 5, spreading across 500 square meters before the Philippine Coast Guard contained it with…

blocks.text: November 6, 2026 | 11:09am

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) deployed oil spill containment equipment following the discovery of 25 liters of used oil affecting 500 square meters of coastal waters at Sitio Naswe, Barangay Ipag, Mariveles, Bataan, on November 5, 2026.
Philippine Coast Guard

MANILA, Philippines — About 25 liters of used oil spilled into the coastal waters of Mariveles, Bataan, on Thursday, November 5, spreading across 500 square meters before the Philippine Coast Guard contained it with booms, the PCG said on Friday, November 6.
The PCG said it received a report of the spill at Sitio Naswe in Barangay Ipag at around 9:30 a.m. Thursday.
Initial findings traced the oil to "washing activities," the PCG said, though the source remains subject to further verification.
By 6:30 p.m., responders had packed 800 kilograms of oil-contaminated debris and spent absorbent materials into 40 sacks, which were placed in temporary storage at a secure site.
For Thursday's cleanup, the PCG mobilized seven absorbent booms and 2,200 absorbent pads in coordination with the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office.
Cleanup operations are scheduled to resume on Friday, the PCG said.

Used oil is classified as hazardous waste under DENR rules implementing Republic Act 6969 or the Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Wastes Control Act of 1990, which govern how such waste is stored, transported and disposed of.

The spill reported yesterday is much smaller than the one from the tanker Terranova, which sank off neighboring Limay in July 2024 with 1.4 million liters of industrial fuel oil and left a slick the PCG measured at 12 to 14 kilometers long.
