articles.title: PR expert says author Steven Galloway had path to rehabilitate reputation
articles.summary: Galloway, a former University of British Columbia writing professor, is suing multiple people who published allegations of sexual assault against him.

image.caption: Bestselling author Steven Galloway is seen in his former office at the University of British Columbia in March 2014. A public relations expert testified on Thursday in an ongoing defamation trial launched by Galloway. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Galloway, a former University of British Columbia writing professor, is suing multiple people who published allegations of sexual assault against him.
Author is suing his accuser and others over statements about him
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 05, 2026 6:10 PM EST | Last Updated: 6 minutes ago

A public relations expert told British Columbia Supreme Court that author and former University of B.C. professor Steven Galloway could have done more to rehabilitate his reputation after he was accused of rape more than a decade ago.

Norman Stowe, a reputation rehabilitation, public relations and crisis management expert, testified on Thursday in the trial of Galloway's defamation lawsuit against his accuser and others who published unproven allegations against him.

"To be blunt, I've worked with clients who had far less going for them than Mr. Galloway in terms of the capacity to go out and defend your reputation or rehabilitate your reputation," said Stowe, a managing partner of the public affairs company Pace Group.

Stowe produced a report for the defence of Galloway's accuser, a woman known as A.B., whose name is subject to a publication ban. He told the court that while he had never worked on a file involving a rape accusation, efforts to rehabilitate someone's reputation involve the same steps regardless of the nature of the issue.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins

The trial heard Stowe's report included examples of other high-profile people who suffered reputational damage, such as Bill Clinton, Martha Stewart and Tiger Woods, but he agreed under cross-examination that allegations against them were not in the same "universe" as a rape accusation.
A.B.'s defence does not allege she was sexually assaulted, rather that she reported the alleged assaults.
Galloway denies the assault claims, and alleges they destroyed his career.

items: Steven Galloway testifies that faculty-student relationships in UBC arts program were common
'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues

blocks.text: The court previously heard from a publishing industry expert who said the author of the hit novel The Cellist of Sarajevo had potentially lost millions of dollars in future income.

Stowe said some of Pace Group's high-profile clients have included the Vancouver Airport Authority following the death of Robert Dziekanski — who died after being Tasered by Mounties at the airport in 2007 — and B.C. Ferries after the sinking of the Queen of the North.
"We have also worked on several cases that involve sexual activities. I can't say much more than that," he said.
Multiple people apologized
The court heard Stowe believed Galloway had a "strong path to reputational rehabilitation" and could have resumed some version of his writing career.
But he conceded under questioning by Galloway's lawyer, Daniel Burnett, that his report incorrectly stated the author had made no efforts to do so.
Burnett said Stewart, Clinton and Woods were all "guilty" of what they'd been accused of, and asked Stowe about a different approach to restoring the reputation of someone who is innocent.

Stowe said he didn't have access to some documents in Galloway's case, including the full report by a retired judge, Mary Ellen Boyd, who found the assault allegations against the author unsubstantiated.

Stowe told the court Boyd's report could have been used as leverage in rehabilitating Galloway's reputation, along with support from those in the literary community who had publicly called for due process for the author.
Bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation trial in 4th week
But Stowe said "there was no plan, no linking these things together to help him get past this and rehabilitate so he could reclaim some part of his personal life and professional life."
Stowe believed Galloway had many opportunities "to bring all these things together, but that never seemed to materialize," he said.
He said he thought the author had "sort of given up," thinking "his life was over."

He agreed that rape allegations are "powerful." But he said Galloway's attempts to refute the claims against him were not part of a plan to rehabilitate his reputation, and the efforts "sort of started and then stalled."

items: UBC prof testifies she acted as a 'conduit' for sex assault allegations against Steven Galloway
Sex assault allegations diminished performance of Steven Galloway's books: industry expert

blocks.text: Stowe said he didn't review social media posts about Galloway, which Burnett said came in "waves … over years and years" leading to the defamation lawsuit.
Stowe's testimony concluded Thursday and defendant Mandi Gray was next to take the stand.
Galloway alleges Gray, an assistant professor at Trent University in Ontario, defamed him in a series of social media posts.
Several people originally named as defendants in Galloway's lawsuit, filed in 2018, have settled with him and offered public apologies.

articles.title: L.A. has a new mayor, and she's a democratic socialist
articles.summary: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation's…

image.caption: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, will be the next mayor of Los Angeles after defeating incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation's second-largest city.
Nithya Raman makes L.A. the 4th U.S. city to elect democratic socialist to top job

The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at city hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.

When she takes office next month, Raman, 45, will join the vanguard of democratic socialists in municipal government. In addition to Mamdani, Janeese Lewis George was elected Tuesday as mayor of Washington, D.C., and Katie Wilson is mayor in Seattle.
Asked about the success of democratic socialists in mayoral contests, U.S. President Donald Trump said "we'll see what happens" but warned the impact of the changes they make might be irreversible.

"There'll be a point at which if people are unhappy, they'll be changed," Trump said in the Oval Office. "But unfortunately, usually that happens so late that you'll never be able to bring back a city or a country or a state. You know — when it goes too far."

Raman's entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, 73, who was once her ally. She said the city had reached a "breaking point" and announced her own candidacy just before the filing deadline.
Bass calls to congratulate victor
Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," Bass said. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us."
Incumbent mayoral candidate Karen Bass, seen at a news conference in L.A. last week, was defeated in the election. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for re-election. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.

As votes were being counted earlier this week, Raman delivered an election night speech Tuesday that marked a campaign coda, summing up voters' frustration with a city that seemed to be adrift, and her vision for the future.

"For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do," she said. "L.A. stopped being a place where we could build things, where we could open things, where we could film things, where we could create things."
She said she would restore "that ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles."
Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.
Raman wants police chief ousted
Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities.
She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years, leaving neighbourhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.
Ballots are inspected on election day Tuesday. (William Liang/The Associated Press)

Raman called Bass's efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors.
Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.

She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.
Raman offered change
Raman was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under Bass.

A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about four in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about three in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.

items: Reality star Spencer Pratt out of L.A. mayor's race as progressive Nithya Raman advances

blocks.text: She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was "not ready for primetime" and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.

"Our city is in crisis," she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicentre of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. "Where is our mayor?" Raman asked.
Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman's views on policing and homelessness as "extreme."
Top Democrats backed Bass

Raman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former U.S. vice president Kamala Harris and former U.S. House speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the city council.
Bass served in the state legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former U.S. president Joe Biden's running mate in 2020.

items: How AI has helped a former reality TV star become a contender for L.A. mayor

blocks.text: In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.

Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.
She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle.

Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions, and serves as a major tourist destination.

articles.title: Ex-DDS cop's testimony sought by ICC prosecutors vs. Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors ask judges to admit preserved testimony from an alleged former member of the Davao Death Squad (DDS), whose evidence they say…
articles.byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 6:34am

THE HAGUE, Netherlands — International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors ask judges to admit preserved testimony from an alleged former member of the Davao Death Squad (DDS), whose evidence they say bears directly on former President Rodrigo Duterte’s alleged criminal responsibility.

In a redacted filing made public dated November 5, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang asked Trial Chamber III to admit 45 transcribed statements and 61 items of associated materials from witness P-0002, identified as a former Davao City police officer.
Those supporting items include P-0002’s handwritten notes, affidavits, photographs, four organizational charts of the DDS structure, police service records, and other personal and official documents.
Unlike recent applications made by the Office of the Prosecutor under Rule 68, this request seeks admission of P-0002’s evidence under Article 69(4) of the Rome Statute.

That article states that the court “may rule on the relevance or admissibility of any evidence” considering its probative value as well as “any prejudice that it may cause to a fair trial or to a fair evaluation of the testimony of a witness.”
DDS structure, alleged policy

Prosecutors described P-0002’s evidence as being “of particular importance” to Duterte’s case, as the witness was a member of the Davao Death Squad. However, the period of his alleged membership is redacted.
His testimony covers Duterte’s alleged individual criminal responsibility and intent, the contextual elements of crimes against humanity during Duterte’s mayoral period, and charged Incident 1.

In the Prosecution’s Trial Brief, Incident 1 refers to the killing of three unidentified alleged drug pushers by DDS members in or around 2013 in San Rafael, Davao City. In this incident, then Davao City Mayor Duterte “instructed police DDS members that there was a job to be done against three alleged drug pushers”.

Prosecutors said P-0002 provided evidence on the origins, structure, and purpose of the DDS, as well as the scope of what the prosecution calls the “Common Plan” in Davao City and the roles of alleged co-perpetrators.
His testimony also concerns the alleged widespread nature of the killings, the targeting of suspected criminals, and the DDS’s alleged modus operandi during the charged period.

According to prosecutors, P-0002’s evidence supports the alleged existence of a policy to “neutralise” suspected criminals in Davao City through measures that included financial incentives, the use of state and civilian forces, and the dissemination of the policy by Duterte to alleged perpetrators.
“Unique opportunity”
Prosecutors interviewed P-0002 from May 10 to 16, 2022, after Pre-Trial Chamber I authorized the interview amid concerns that his evidence might later become unavailable.
The Chamber found a “unique opportunity” to interview P-0002 and a significant risk that his evidence “may not be subsequently available.”
A defense counsel appointed to protect the interests of any future accused was present during the interview, along with counsel for P-0002.

The filing says prosecutors were informed of a development concerning P-0002 in June 2024, but the details are redacted. It later states that “P-0002 is no longer available,” but does not expound or clarify.
Prosecutors argued that the preserved testimony should be admitted under Article 69 because it was obtained through a judicially authorized evidence-preservation procedure.

They said it could alternatively be admitted under Rule 68(2)(c) of the ICC Rules of Procedure – or about prior recorded testimony from “a person who has subsequently died, must be presumed dead, or is, due to obstacles that cannot be overcome with reasonable diligence, unavailable to testify orally.”
Trial Chamber III has yet to rule on the request.
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed during his terms as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
His trial is scheduled to begin on November 30. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Fox News suffers ratings slump on bleak election night for Republicans
articles.summary: In early, preliminary figures, the news channel trailed several other networks in prime-time viewership

blocks.text: On a midterm election night that was a huge disappointment for Republicans, with Democrats taking control of the US House and Senate, the country’s most prominent conservative television network seemingly felt the brunt of viewer disillusionment with Donald Trump and his party, according to final audience numbers released on Thursday.

The Fox News Channel, which often leads among all news networks in viewership on election nights, fell behind two top broadcasters on Tuesday. According to ratings dating from the Nielsen firm, the network averaged 4.3 million total viewers between 8 and 11pm, behind broadcast networks NBC (6.7 million viewers) and ABC (5.2 million viewers), though it edged out fellow cable networks CNN (4.1 million viewers) and MS Now (3.7 million viewers). Fox News handedly defeat CBS News, which attracted just 2.8 million viewers. CNN performed better in the 25-to-54 age demographic prized by advertisers, besting Fox News, MS Now and CBS.
Originally, preliminary viewership numbers released Wednesday put Fox News behind both CNN and MS Now in total viewership in primetime.

Overall, the big six television networks averaged nearly 27 million total viewers during prime-time election coverage, up from 22.215 million total viewers in 2022. During those 2022 elections, Fox News averaged 7.422 million viewers, meaning its viewership slipped about 41% on Tuesday.

With Trump reaching historic levels of unpopularity, Fox News has seen some viewers tune out in recent weeks. Last month, the network’s viewership was down 27% compared with the same month last year in total day viewers, though it still handily defeated CNN and MS Now. Lachlan Murdoch, the chief executive of parent company Fox Corp, acknowledged “viewer fatigue” in an earnings call on Monday.

Trump, who criticized Fox throughout election night and blamed the network for his party’s losses, poked fun at the network’s October figures in a Truth Social post, chalking up the decline to the channel’s industry-standard practice of booking Democratic candidates for interviews.

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” he wrote on Tuesday evening. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me – My numbers are better than they have ever been.”
This story was updated on Thursday afternoon to reflect final viewership figures released by Nielsen.

articles.title: Rush announces week-long concert series in Las Vegas
articles.summary: Rush may be currently delighting fans while on tour, but the Canadian Music Hall of Famers are already prepping for the next high-profile gig soon after its wraps: a week-long residency at immersive…

image.caption: On the heels of their current, much-lauded tour, iconic prog-rockers Rush will dive straight into another high-profile gig: a week-long residency at immersive Las Vegas venue Sphere next year. (Chris Young/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Rush may be currently delighting fans while on tour, but the Canadian Music Hall of Famers are already prepping for the next high-profile gig soon after its wraps: a week-long residency at immersive Las Vegas venue Sphere.
Rock icons vow to 'concoct some new madness' for shows 'to please our fans both visually and viscerally'

Iconic prog-rockers Rush may be currently delighting fans on a much lauded international tour, but the Canadian Music Hall of Famers are already prepping for the next high-profile gig: a week-long residency at the Sphere.
On Thursday, Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson announced the five-concert series, dubbed Elevate from the Norm, set for late May at the immersive Las Vegas venue.
The dates are mere weeks after the scheduled mid-April finale of Rush's Fifty Something Tour, which is taking the reunited band across North and South America, Europe and the U.K.
German drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold, who have been performing with the Lee and Lifeson, will also join them for the Sphere shows.

Lee revealed that when he first heard about the dome-shaped venue and its wraparound high-tech LED displays, he imagined it a perfect match for "the kind of visual attitude" of Rush's concerts, even though they weren't touring anymore.
"Life is nothing if not surprising and now, here we are, living and touring in the present tense and we are able to make that particular dream come true," he said in a statement.
Rush members honour late drummer Neil Peart at TIFF
Rush's Sphere setlist will include both greatest hits and fan favourites, he said, to celebrate their musical legacy as well as the life of virtuoso drummer and lyricist Neil Peart, who died in 2020.

The band is working to "concoct some new madness to suit this incredible venue," Lee noted, anticipating the chance "to please our fans both visually and viscerally from wherever they might fly in from."
The shows could be just the thing to lure Canadians back to Las Vegas, which has seen visits from Canada — the state of Nevada's largest source of international tourists — plummet.
Las Vegas pulls out all the stops to win back Canadians

Since opening in fall 2023, Sphere has hosted top recording artists and major shows, from opening act U2 to the Backstreet Boys, Phish to No Doubt, with Metallica, The Eagles and John Mayer among the latest set for that spherical stage.
VIP and travel packages for Rush's Elevate from the Norm shows go on sale Friday, while the artist presale begins Nov. 11. General public tickets go on sale starting two days after that.

articles.title: 15 patients released, 5 still hospitalized following bus crash near Mackenzie, B.C.
articles.summary: WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code…

image.caption: The University Hospital of Northern B.C. in Prince George declared a code orange Wednesday afternoon following a major bus crash that threatened to overwhelm its resources. (Tom Popyk/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code orange.
WorkSafeBC investigating alongside RCMP after 'chaotic' crash
Northern Health says 15 people have been released from hospital and five are still receiving care following a major bus crash near Mackenzie, north of Prince George, B.C., Wednesday.

WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the northbound shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code orange. No other vehicles were involved.
Six air ambulances and six ground ambulances treated and transported 20 patients with injuries ranging from minor to serious, according to B.C. Emergency Health Services.

Northern Health says all 20 patients were taken to hospital in either Prince George or Mackenzie, with fifteen being treated and released. Four others remain in care locally, while one was airlifted to another facility elsewhere in the province.
About 20 people hospitalized after bus crash near Mackenzie
Updates on their conditions are not being shared by BCEHS, Northern Health or RCMP, who all cited patient privacy.

items: About 20 people injured, several seriously, in northern B.C. bus crash: police

blocks.text: Operations at both hospitals have since returned to normal, with Northern Health thanking "the physicians, nurses, first responders and other health professionals in Mackenzie and Prince George whose rapid and highly-professional response saved lives and prevented this tragic incident from taking an even greater toll on the victims."
'Nothing has been ruled out': Police
B.C. Highway Patrol has taken control of the investigation, with RCMP saying that while no arrests have been made, "the cause of the crash is still uncertain" and "nothing has been ruled out."
WorkSafeBC is also investigating with a spokesperson saying they are "working with law enforcement partners to establish an understanding of the factors related to this incident."
The shuttle bus was carrying workers subcontracted by Iren, a multinational data centre company with facilities in Mackenzie and Prince George.

articles.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he'll commute all death row sentences to life in prison
articles.summary: California governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the…

image.caption: California Governor Gavin Newsom says he will commute the sentences of all 548 death row inmates in California to life in prison. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

California governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."
There are currently 548 people on death row in the state, the highest number in the U.S.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no possibility of parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."

In an open letter, Newsom says his decision comes after three decades of openly opposing state-sanctioned executions. He issued a moratorium on all inmate executions in the state in 2019, but said it wasn't enough as their death sentences remained intact.
There are currently 548 people on death row in California, which Newsom describes as "the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere."
California last put a ⁠prisoner to death in ⁠2006, when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was ‌governor.

Newsom's decision, which he calls the most difficult of his career, comes just months before the end of his eight-year term as governor, and amid speculation he will launch a bid to run as the Democratic candidate for president in 2028.
Newsom speaks with incarcerated men at San Quentin State Prison in San Quentin, Calif., in March 2023. (Eric Risberg/The Associated Press)
Requires state Supreme Court approval

The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court's approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70 per cent, according to numbers provided by Newsom's office.
California voters rejected a ballot measure in 2016 that would have repealed the death penalty in the state.
"I recognize the limits of this clemency action," Newsom wrote, "which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences."
Repealing the law rests with the legislature and voters, but he says that, as governor, he has clemency authority "for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice."
"For me," he said, "this is that moment."

Last month, the California District Attorneys Association sent a letter to Newsom expressing "grave concerns" about the possibility he would commute the sentences, warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional anguish on victims' families.

"Every death sentence in California represents an individual case in which a jury heard the evidence, considered the circumstances and determined that the most serious punishment under our law was warranted," association President Jeannine M. Pacioni said.
"To simply erase all those judgments with the stroke of a pen, without considering the facts of each case or the families affected, would be a profound disservice to the administration of justice."
Newsom said he is aware his decision will surface painful memories for the families of victims of crime.
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," Newsom wrote.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, seen here in December 2007, survived two state-sanctioned execution attempts in September. (J. Miles Cary/ Knoxville News Sentinel/USA Today Network/Reuters)
Renewed debate over capital punishment

The debate over capital punishment in the U.S. intensified recently after Tennessee's failed execution of condemned killer Christa Pike, ‌who survived two attempts to inject her with lethal drugs on Sept. 30.
Pike was hospitalized afterward and was sent back to prison on Oct. 10.

The death penalty received further scrutiny after U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to ​livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more ⁠than 30 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in ⁠Texas on Nov. 5, 2009.
U.S. President Donald Trump later ruled out a livestream ⁠of ⁠the execution, but Hasan is still ​scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
LISTEN | The debate over the death penalty:
As It Happens1:14:47A botched lethal injection reignites death penalty debate
ACLU welcomes move
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded Newsom's announcement.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," executive director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California's death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.

In 2023, Newsom announced plans to transform San Quentin prison, a facility in the San Francisco Bay Area known for maintaining the largest number of prisoners on death row in the country, into a place where inmates could be rehabilitated and receive job training before returning to society.
That work was completed earlier this year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Stephanie Hogan is a digital producer with CBC News, based in Toronto. She writes on a variety of subjects, with an interest in politics, health and the arts. She was previously political editor for The National and worked in various roles in TV and radio news.
With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Canada's new budget proposes $5B for culture. Here's where it would go
articles.summary: The Carney government's new budget proposes roughly $5 billion over the next five years toward several initiatives to promote Canadian culture, including building new recreational facilities and ice…

image.caption: People arrive in atrium of the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa on Saturday, July 18, 2020. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Carney government's new budget proposes roughly $5 billion over the next five years toward several initiatives to promote Canadian culture, including building new recreational facilities and ice rinks, supporting national museums and permanently making their admissions free for people 25 and younger.
New money to support national museums, building recreation facilities, ice rinks
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 05, 2026 4:06 PM EST | Last Updated: 22 minutes ago
That figure includes more funding for CBC/Radio-Canada and the Local Journalism Initiative.

"Being sovereign means building a country where Canadian culture in all its diversity and creativity thrives," the 2026 budget reads, adding Ottawa is "investing in the stores, places and experiences that connect Canadians to their country and to one another."

The budget proposes providing $1.5 billion over nine years through the Build Communities Strong Fund to support the construction, expansion, retrofit and rehabilitation of community recreational facilities and ice rinks across the country.
Budget focused on affordability, opportunity and sovereignty, Carney says

It also intends to provide $783.1 million over five years, starting this year, to support Canada's national museums, the National Battlefields Commission, the National Arts Centre and Library and Archives Canada.

"This investment will help repair and renew aging facilities, protect national collections and sustain the exhibitions, performances and services that connect Canadians to our history and culture," the budget says.
The national museum funding includes $46.3 million over five years for permanent, year-round free admission for children and youth under 25, plus $11.5 million ongoing.
Other notable items include $76 million in 2027-28 to renew the Canada Strong Pass for another summer.
Ottawa launches 'Canada Strong Pass' to promote domestic tourism | Hanomansing Tonight
The pass gives people free entry to all sites operated by Parks Canada, and free or discounted Via Rail trips depending on age.

Ottawa is proposing a $300-million Canada 160 Fund, an initiative to mark the country's 160th anniversary. The fund will support Canada's Heritage Minutes, the Trans Canada Trail and other community spaces.

items: History, war museums to slash dozens of positions
New Canada Strong Pass offers discounts on parks, museums, camping and train travel

blocks.text: It also intends to provide $15.9 million over four years, starting next year, and $2.1 million ongoing to Veterans Affairs Canada to "acquire, remediate and operate" the National Field of Honour military cemetery.
There is a proposal to provide $11.4 million over three years, starting this year, to Veterans Affairs Canada to support the commemoration of defining moments in Canada's military history.
Funding for journalism, media, artists
The budget pitches an additional $300 million over two years, starting this year, to CBC/Radio-Canada to "strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country."

It proposes $134 million over four years, starting next year, and $41 million ongoing to Canadian Heritage for the Local Journalism Initiative, which is meant to help organizations hire or pay journalists in underserved communities.
The federal government also wants to extend the enhanced 35 per cent Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit — set to expire next month — to 2028.
TV crew pass a CBC logo at their headquarters in Toronto, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Print journalism currently has access to the credit, and Ottawa wants to expand the credit to "qualifying private audio and audiovisual news organizations, in line with support provided to news organizations that produce written news."
The budget says the extended and expanded credit would cost an estimated $501 million over five years, starting this year, and $85 million ongoing.
The budget also proposes to establish a free national digital book collection. The federal government aims to provide $32.2 million over four years, starting next year, to get the collection started.
According to the budget, the digital collection would launch with at least 200 titles in 2027, then grow to more than 2,000 titles with capacity for up to two million loans annually by 2031.

A man walks past a part of the Emily Carr collection titled, "Fresh Seeing a French Modernism and West Coast," on exhibit at the Royal BC Museum in Victoria, B.C., on Oct. 28, 2020. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
The federal government says it will consult with Canadians and the cultural sector on a new Canada Creative Credit — which is expected to take the form of a non-refundable personal income tax credit.

The budget says when combined with the basic personal amount every filer has exempted from income tax, artists could have up to $45,000 of annual net business income derived from original and creative works exempted.
Details on the Canada Creative Credit will be announced in the 2027 spring economic update, the budget said.
Money for ocean preservation
The federal government classifies its proposed investments in Canada's oceans under its cultural plan.

To that end, the 2026 budget pitches establishing and operating two additional National Marine Conservation Areas. Ottawa is proposing $282.7 million over 11 years, starting next year, and $18 million ongoing to Parks Canada toward the initiative.

items: Carney announces $1.2B in funding to protect oceans as major projects loom

blocks.text: Plus, the budget proposes $9.2 million to Parks Canada and $10.5 million to Fisheries and Oceans Canada to support feasibility assessments for up to three additional National Marine Conservation Areas in the North.
Both those sums would come over four years, starting next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Lopez Steven is an associate producer for CBC's The House and a digital writer with CBC Politics. He was also a 2024 Joan Donaldson Scholar and a graduate of Carleton University. You can reach him at benjamin.steven@cbc.ca or find him on X at @bensteven_s.

articles.title: From gas to groceries, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?
articles.summary: The 2026 budget increases payments for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and expands a tax credit for low-wage workers. But the affordability measures are mostly for the short term, and…

image.caption: Loblaws customers shop at a Toronto-area grocery store on March 6, 2025. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

The 2026 budget increases payments for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and expands a tax credit for low-wage workers. But the affordability measures are mostly for the short term, and took a back seat to measures aimed at boosting investment.
Push to spur investment overshadows affordability moves: economist
From a grocery benefit expansion to rental assistance and payments for more low-wage workers, Thursday's federal budget includes a number of measures aimed at making life more affordable.
But they were still eclipsed by a focus on investment.
One of the main direct pocketbook measures is a top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit — a pre-existing program that gives quarterly payments to Canadians with low and modest incomes.

The top-up will increase those payments by 50 per cent for the 2026-27 program year. Combined with previous increases, a single person could get up to $1,290. A couple with two children could get up to $2,570.

items: Carney's 2nd budget earmarks billions for affordability and Canadian sovereignty
Budget 2026: Ottawa bets on investment, major projects to boost Canada's economy

blocks.text: The government says the program will give Canadians collectively $4.1 billion more in support to help pay for essentials.

More low-income workers will also get benefit payments to help them make ends meet. Those who make a minimum of $3,000 annually get a refundable tax credit under the Canada Workers Benefit, but that threshold is being lowered to $500 for all workers. The budget also increases those credits slightly, to $1,859 for single individuals who don't have kids and $3,143 for families.

Other measures aimed at bringing down costs were already announced. The government suspended the excise tax on fuel — which saves Canadians about 10 cents a litre on the cost of gasoline — in April, and later extended that to the end of January 2027. The tax will come back at a 50 per cent rate until the end of March 2027 and then return to its regular level.
In all, the budget shows the government spending $5.3 billion on that relief at the pumps.
Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel
Overall, the federal government's fiscal plan pledges $22 billion for new spending on affordability measures.

But aside from that direct spending on things like groceries and gas — measures that will support Canadians in the short term — economist Armine Yalnizyan says there's little in the budget for everyday people.
"It's not like they're doing nothing," Yalnizyan said. "But the short answer is Canadians are going to need a lot of patience because this budget is not there to support them."

The biggest-ticket spending on affordability is related to housing, with $11.2 billion dedicated to ending homelessness within 10 years. That money would help build supportive and transitional housing and provide support to facilities that care for people in a mental health or substance abuse crisis.

To help low-income renters, the government is also renewing the Canada Housing Benefit for 10 years to support Canadians with direct monthly rental assistance, to the tune of $1.7 billion starting in the 2028-29 fiscal year.

Yalnizyan said the pledge to end homelessness is a welcome one — as is the commitment to extend the ban on foreign purchases of rental properties to January 2026. But the housing benefit doesn't go far enough, she says, and the money to fund new housing projects won't benefit Canadians for years to come.

New homes under construction in the community of Upper Caledon East. The federal budget pledged $11.2 billion to end homelessness, as well as more money to build non-market housing and regular homes. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
"There is money there for it but it's not coming through fast enough," Yalnizyan said. "There's too much wait and see, come and talk to us later," Yalnizyan said.

Those affordability measures are also eclipsed by tax cuts and investments in infrastructure and other major projects. The previously announced productivity mega-deduction alone accounts for $36 billion worth of spending, compared to $22 billion overall for affordability.
Rather than boosting everyday Canadians, Yalnizyan says the budget is focused on catalyzing investment and attracting new spending within Canada.
"It's not a bad budget for all of that, but they've left out the people," Yalnizyan said.

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. articles.title: Austrian tycoon Rene Benko sentenced to 2 years in prison for fraud
articles.summary: Austrian businessman Rene Benko, who suffered a major fall from grace after his real estate empire, Signa Holding, went bust, was handed two more years in prison.

image.caption: Rene Benko is under investigation for possible crimes related to the fall of his real estate empire, Signa HoldingImage: Angelika Warmuth/REUTERS

blocks.text: Rene Benko, an Austrian businessman whose legacy as a property tycoon collapsed with the fall of his real estate empire Signa Holding three years ago, was sentenced to two more years in prison on Thursday.

The Innsbruck Regional Court found Beko guilty of defrauding €5 million from the private foundation of Austrian industrialist Hans Peter Haselsteiner. The payment from Haselsteiner arrived just weeks before Signa Holding declared insolvency.

It was the third criminal proceeding against Banko, coming after two earlier convictions. He was sentenced in the first case in October 2025 on charges of insolvency related fraud. In September 2026, he received a 30-month term for harming creditors.
The new sentence against Benko, 49, comes just ‌three weeks ⁠after ⁠he was released to house arrest to serve out a previous conviction.

blocks.caption: Rene Benko with his lawyers at the trial Image: Johann Groder/Expa/APA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Benko's lawyer said he would assess whether to appeal the conviction over the weekend.
Benko was acquitted on a second charge that he had hidden a luxury rifle worth €80,000 from creditors.
The fall of Signa Holding
Benko was once thought to have been a wunderkind for having established himself as a self-made entrepreneur after dropping out of college.
At its peak, Signa Holdings accumulated a portfolio worth more than $30 billion, with stakes in New York's Chrysler Building and Berlin's KaDeWe department store.
In 2023, Signa Holdings declared bankruptcy, dealing a blow to a myriad of European property investors and others.
The fall of Signa was considered the single biggest financial earthquake to have hit the European property market since the global financial crisis of 2008.

articles.title: British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital
articles.summary:
Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital

A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic…

blocks.text: A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.

The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London.

Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: “UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.”

A humanitarian organisation sent the doctor to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared in May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. It has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, and last month Nigeria confirmed a case in its capital, Abuja.

People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus. Initial symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding.
after newsletter promotion

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK previously. A case in 1976 was from a laboratory needle incident, and the three others involved health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

articles.title: California governor commutes death sentences for all 548 people on death row
articles.summary: California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates in the US.

blocks.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead with life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.

The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been killed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.

Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".

He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US.

On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

articles.title: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
articles.summary: There is no hard evidence so far linking airline bomb threats to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups.

blocks.text: The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.

In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.
They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not be real.

It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.

Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.
So is Russia behind this?

There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.
Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.

Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?
But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.
There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".
That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.
Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.

But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.

For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

articles.title: Post-secondary students across Ontario walk out of classrooms to protest province's cuts to OSAP, tuition hike
articles.summary: University and college students across Ontario are protesting rising tuition fees and the province's cuts to the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) in a provincewide walkout Thursday.

image.caption: Students across Ontario are protesting the province's changes to OSAP and tuition fees on Thursday. (Paul Smith/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New
University and college students across Ontario are protesting rising tuition fees and the province's cuts to the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) in a provincewide walkout Thursday.
Province-wide walkouts happening across multiple campuses Thursday
University and college students across Ontario are protesting rising tuition fees and the province's changes to the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) in a province-wide walkout Thursday.
"Students have had enough of being asked to pay more, borrow more and accept less," Cyrielle Ngeleka, chair of the Canadian Federation of Students (CFS) Ontario said at Queen's Park Thursday.
"We have witnessed hundreds of programs cut, student services stretched, and the cost of education pushed further onto the backs of students and their families."

CFS Ontario is the largest student organization in the province, representing over 350,000 students. The walkouts are part of the federation's "Hands Off Our Education!" campaign, with protests sprouting on several campuses, including York University, the University of Guelph, Trent University and University of Windsor.

items: Students brace for debt, reconsider studies as OSAP cuts take effect

blocks.text: The protest comes after the province lifted a seven-year tuition freeze earlier in the year, which allowed universities and colleges to increase fees by up to two per cent each year over the next three years.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government has also been under fire for the larger part of the year after announcing changes to OSAP in February, citing "unsustainable" costs.

Changes to the student assistance program meant non-repayable grants were reduced from a maximum of 85 per cent to 25 per cent, while the percentage of funds given as loans increased. Many students have said scaled-back OSAP grants will saddle them with high debt loads amid economic uncertainty.
The province has previously defended the changes, and highlighted its $6.4-billion funding for Ontario's colleges and universities, to be rolled out over the next four years.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said in February this funding will help institutions provide competitive programs, high standards of education and be “resilient” to growing demands in the future.
CBC Toronto has requested additional comment from Quinn on Thursday's protests.
Education is a right: York University student

At York University, students and supporters gathered at 9 a.m. with signs reading "OSAP weaves futures, not baskets," (in response to a previous comment from Ford) and "Education should not be a debt sentence."
Symone Lennon, president of the York Federation of Students, shouted "Tax on students" into a microphone as the crowd replied "Vote it down!"

"Every single student deserves to be here," Lennon told CBC Toronto. "The message is simple. It's not only fund OSAP, it is simply fund our education as students because we have a right to be here and it is not a privilege."
York University student Symone Lennon, who is also president of the York Federation of Students, was protesting Ontario's changes to OSAP on Thursday. (Paul Smith/CBC)
Lennon says one of her friends was forced to take time off from attending university because of changes to OSAP, and she herself is nervous about her future in a competitive job market.
"The future is looking quite bleak right now, for not only just me, but a number of students," she said.
Recent York University graduate Sam Jean told CBC Toronto that he had heard some high schoolers were deferring post-secondary education because of changes to OSAP.
"It's just completely pulled the rug out from a whole generation of students," said Jean. "A lot of students acutely feel like we don't have a future."
Opposition parties support protesting students
Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said in a news release she stands with students protesting Ford's changes to OSAP.

"Doug Ford has spent this year attacking students," said Stiles. "We called on [Ford] to come up with a plan to provide immediate relief to students who need financial assistance. He and his government refused.
"They've made it clear that they have no interest in helping Ontario students ... Now, the Premier has no choice but to hear their voices."
Ontario Greens Leader Mike Schreiner expressed the party's support for university students in a statement Thursday.

"Young people are struggling to get by in an economy stacked against them. It’s never been harder to get a job and a record number of youth are being forced to choose between a roof and food," he said.
"Now more than ever, we should be working to shrink student debt and remove barriers for young people — not sticking them with tens of thousands of dollars of debt."
Schreiner called on the Ford government to reverse changes to OSAP, remove interest on student loans and unlock frozen funds so low and middle-income students can access non-repayable grants.

In addition to changes to student assistance to college and universities in Ontario, the provincial government has recently frozen OSAP funding for private career colleges after an audit found "serious concerns."
Quinn has said the provincial government will bring back the program when it has the "confidence" and "guardrails in place" to ensure financial aid is being used in good faith.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Amy van den Berg is a writer and editor at CBC News, based in Toronto. You can reach out to her at amy.van.den.berg@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after review, sexual assault allegations
articles.summary: Months after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on the set of Married at First Sight UK, the results of an external review have prompted Channel 4 to decide not…

image.caption: Married at First Sight UK will not return to Channel 4, and the show's budget will be reinvested in new programming, following the results of an external review of contributor welfare. (Channel 4)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Months after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on the set of Married at First Sight UK, the results of an external review have prompted Channel 4 to decide not to bring the show back.
Channel 4 says show will not return after 3 female contestants alleged misconduct
Britain's Channel 4 says it will not bring back Married at First Sight UK, following the results of an external review into contributor welfare.
It was commissioned after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on set.
The show follows strangers matched by relationship experts who meet for the first time at the altar, take part in a mock wedding ceremony and move in together as newlyweds.
The U.K. version of the program was considered to be a massive ratings juggernaut for Channel 4, and ran for 10 seasons.

In May, BBC's current affairs program Panorama spoke to two women who said they were raped by their on-screen husbands, and a third who alleged her on-screen husband subjected her to a non-consensual sexual act.

items: Married at First Sight UK pulls episodes after brides allege sexual assault by co-stars

blocks.text: The men denied the allegations. In June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.
Channel 4 commissioned a review tasked with examining whether the show's welfare protocols met its duty of care obligations — and whether those protocols needed to be changed.
The results of that review, released Thursday, found the show's welfare protocols were extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard — though in some isolated incidents, not fully implemented.
Measures to improve welfare

The final report also included recommendations to improve the welfare of Married at First Sight UK cast members — including putting couples in separate bedrooms on wedding night and honeymoon, reviewing the frequency with which couples are asked about the physical side of their relationship, and removing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week.

It also suggested installing CCTV and sound recording equipment in all areas of the apartments to be monitored 24/7 by a welfare-trained team, and providing two lockable ensuite bedrooms for cast members.
Channel 4 headquarters in London, U.K. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

"MAFS UK has been enjoyed by millions of viewers, made possible by the willingness of its contributors to embrace the social experiment at the heart of the show and the many talented people involved in its production," said Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra in a statement.
She thanked the team for its efforts to protect the welfare of contributors, but said "the series will not return to Channel 4, with the show’s budget reinvested in distinctive new programming."
Dogra also repeated her apology to the female cast members who came forward with their allegations.

"This review did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama program, but I would like to repeat that I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt."
She said she hopes Channel 4's swift action demonstrates "our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards."
The show is part of an international reality-TV franchise with editions in countries including the U.S. and Australia.
CBC News has not had any response to questions about whether those shows will continue.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.
with files from Kayla McLean

articles.title: Americans voted against Trump's Iran war. Gulf countries hope that means an end to the conflict
articles.summary: The US midterm results showed how unpopular Donald Trump's Iran war is. Now, Gulf countries, trapped for months in the middle of the war between the US and Iran, see reason for optimism.

image.caption: Celebrations in Tehran: Some experts suggest Iran was determined not to give Donald Trump any concessions before the midterms, so that he remained under pressure — now they may be more willing to negotiateImage: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: After his party's resounding defeat in the US midterm elections this week, President Donald Trump conceded that the war with Iran had likely played a part.

"I think a part of it was Iran, but, at the same time, people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, conceding that US voters were unwilling to accept the impact of the war on gas prices.
Observers say the United States and Israel had been holding off on major attacks on Iran until after both had held elections.
At the end of October, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was already warning Gulf state governments to brace for a short, intense military campaign after the midterms.
Could conflict escalate again?

While foreign policy is a US president's purview, analysts have pointed out that a Congress controlled by the Democratic party could ostensibly withhold funding for Trump's military expeditions. However newly-elected Democratic politicians won't take their seats until early next year.

blocks.caption: The US has been moving military assets into the Middle East and limited attacks on Iran have been ongoingImage: Menelaos Hadjicostis/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: As two US professors of political science wrote for Foreign Affairs magazine this week, past American presidents, like Trump, who become "lame ducks" — that is, a president who loses control of Congress and can't run for another term — have often ramped up international interventions.

"As they think about their legacy, lame ducks often turn to foreign policy, where the power of the presidency allows them to act unfettered by pesky domestic politics," they explained. And one of the places where Trump is most likely to act is Iran, the professors argued.
On the other hand, Trump also told several media outlets that he was in "no rush" to start bombing Iran again.
Opinions on Iran's next moves are also divided.

The Iranians have said they're ready for any attack and rhetoric from senior leaders indicates they may be willing to strike a wider range of targets than previously. That could include regional energy and economic infrastructure and even undersea telecommunications cabling or data centers.

If Iran thinks there is an existential threat to its leadership, then "all bets are off," Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, or MEI, and an expert on Iran, said during a virtual briefing hosted by MEI this week. "I think they will target differently in the Gulf states [this time] … so it really depends on how all this unfolds."
But other experts believe Iran was deliberately holding out to pressure Trump before the midterms. Now the election is over, the Iranians may be more willing to negotiate a peace deal.
Unwilling participants
All this leaves the Gulf states, who have been the main targets of Iranian attacks since the conflict began, in a difficult position.

"We find ourselves drawn within a crisis that we worked diplomatically very hard to try to avert," Anwar Gargash, a foreign policy adviser to United Arab Emirates leadership, said at a security conference in Bahrain last weekend, the Manama Dialogue hosted by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS. "We are clearly seeking a political off-ramp."

Qatar has been trying to negotiate between the US and Iran but has also been conducting emergency drills at its airport. The Emiratis have been doing similar drills. And Saudi Arabia is looking at a war on two fronts: The oil-rich state is already under attack from the Houthi militia in neighboring Yemen. Even Egypt has reacted, reportedly strengthening air defenses around the Suez Canal.
Still, no matter what happens next, the US-Israel-Iran war has already made Gulf states evaluate defense partnerships with the US. Rather than making them safe, US bases have made them a target.

"There is widespread disappointment across the region with the US over the folly of the war, the erratic nature of Washington's military and diplomatic conduct, and its decision to prioritize Israel's defense over that of its Gulf partners," Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow at the IISS, told news agency Bloomberg this week. "If the US liberation of Kuwait in 1991 was the moment that established America's role in the region, the 2026 war may be remembered as the moment that undid it."
Replacing America?
Gulf states are widening their outreach with, for example, the UAE getting closer to Israel and the Saudis entering the Mecca defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey.

"The Gulf states have already moved toward strategic autonomy and self-reliance," Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London, wrote for online outlet Middle East Eye this week. "A lame-duck Trump will speed that process."
That's even though a Democrat-led Congress might make the US a slightly more reliable partner again.
Krieg argues that Gulf states should come together to pressure the US not to attack Iran and then negotiate a non-aggression pact with Iran — without US involvement.

Whether that kind of unity is possible in the Gulf is dubious, Ryan Crocker, a former US ambassador to the region and distinguished fellow with MEI, replied to a question from DW during the MEI's online briefing.

blocks.caption: Reevaluating the relationship? Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (left) and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at a recent G20 meeting in the USImage: Megan Varner/AFP

blocks.text: "I'm afraid that meaningful Gulf unity is not coming to a theater near us anytime soon," Crocker said. The Qataris remain untrusting because of how other Gulf states acted against them in 2017. And, he added, "there are well known differences between Saudi Arabia and the UAE we see in Sudan [and] in Yemen, and, of course, the profound differences … on relations with Israel. So I would not expect any meaningful moves toward [Gulf] security cooperation."
What's more likely in the long term is Gulf states eventually coming to some kind of understanding with Iran.

"The Gulf states understand that they probably can't buy their security only from Washington, and that they're going to have to buy it, to some degree, by some kind of a relationship with Tehran," the MEI's Harrison added. "It's inevitable. Geography reigns."

What that sort of non-aggression pact looks like remains to be seen, he added. That's why one of the big concerns for Gulf leaders now, is the conflict escalating again to a point where the path back to some sort of diplomacy is lost, Harrison concluded.
